assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL NEW ENGLAND YACHT CLUB, shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE of the building: no wall, no window, no door, no porch post and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE BUILDING FACES THE WATER AT THE TOP OF THE FRAME. THREE THINGS MAKE THIS A CLUB AND NOT A LARGE HOUSE, and all three must be present. (1) THE DECK, AND EVERY GOOD YACHT CLUB HAS ONE. On the WATER side of the building — the top of the frame — a broad open TIMBER DECK runs the full width of the clubhouse and reaches out toward the water about two thirds as deep as the building. IT IS OPEN TO THE SKY AND HAS NO ROOF, so unlike every other building in this town you are looking at its FLOOR: pale weathered planks laid straight across, board by board, several visibly paler than their neighbours. That expanse of open planking beside a shingled roof is the clearest possible cue that this is a club and not a house — nothing else on this shore shows a floor. Around its three outer edges runs a RAILING: a thin dark line for the top rail with a row of short evenly spaced dark TICKS just inside it, one per baluster, seen END-ON and foreshortened to almost nothing. Ticks, never uprights. At one end a short flight of STEPS runs down and out as three or four narrow parallel bars. THE DECK IS BUSY AND HAPPY — this is where the club sits and watches the racing, and it should look like it. Along the seaward rail, FOUR ADIRONDACK CHAIRS in a row, evenly spaced and all facing out to the water: seen from above each is an unmistakable little shape, a WEDGE of narrow parallel slats wider at the front than the back, with two broad flat ARM boards standing out either side, in pale weathered timber. Further in on the deck, TWO ROUND TABLES, each a disc of pale timber with three small dark chair-backs set round it like commas. OVER EACH TABLE A PARASOL, seen from directly above as a CIRCLE: a shallow cone of canvas with eight straight seams running from the rim to a small dark cap at the centre, its panels alternating warm cream and deep harbour green, hiding most of the table beneath it — which is what proves it stands above. The two parasols are at slightly different angles. Everything on the deck is furniture and nothing is a person: no figures anywhere. (2) THE RACE COMMITTEE DECK, standing on the main ridge: a small rectangular railed platform, flat-topped, its floor a pale deck, with the same handrail-and-ticks treatment and no wider than a third of the ridge. (3) THE CLUB BURGEE, PAINTED FLAT ON THE ROOF, and it is the identity of the whole asset. THERE IS NO FLAGPOLE AND NO FLYING FLAG ANYWHERE IN THIS PICTURE. The club's burgee is painted directly onto the roof shingles as an aerial marking — the way a boathouse or a hangar carries its mark for the benefit of anyone passing — so it is PAINT ON A FLAT SURFACE and lies perfectly in the plane of the roof. It has no thickness, no pole, no halyard, no shadow, no ripple, no curl and no lift: it is a flat coloured shape on the shingles, exactly as a painted line on a road is. Where the roof's slope changes tone at the ridge, THE PAINT CHANGES TONE WITH IT, because paint takes the light of the surface it sits on. IT IS DRAWN LARGE, spanning about half the length of the main roof and centred on the seaward slope so it faces the water. ⚠️ ITS GEOMETRY IS EXACT AND IS MEASURED FROM THE CLUB'S OWN BURGEE; copy these numbers rather than drawing a flag from memory. IT IS A CLEAN ISOSCELES TRIANGLE lying on its side, about ONE AND A HALF TIMES AS LONG AS ITS UPRIGHT EDGE IS TALL (1.45 to 1) — a stubby broad pennant, NOT a long thin streamer. Its tall edge is at the left and its two long edges are PERFECTLY STRAIGHT, tapering evenly to ONE SHARP POINT at the right: at the halfway station it is exactly HALF as tall as its left edge, at three quarters along exactly a QUARTER. No swallowtail, no forked or notched tail, no wave, no fold. THE DESIGN IS FIXED: a NAVY field around #1C2E6E, crossed by a single BROAD vertical RED band around #D83839. ⚠️ THE BAND'S PLACE AND WIDTH ARE MEASURED: it begins about a QUARTER of the way along from the tall edge and ends about TWO THIRDS along, covering a good TWO FIFTHS of the whole length — a broad band dominating the middle, never a thin stripe near the edge. Navy shows either side of it, and the navy behind the point is the wider of the two. Centred on that red band, a WHITE PAW PRINT — one larger rounded pad below and four small oval toes arched above it. No other mark, no letter, no word, no number, no star. The paint is slightly weathered, its edges a touch soft where the shingle texture shows faintly through. ON THE MAIN ROOF, otherwise plain: one squat brick CHIMNEY at one end of the ridge, pointing at the camera and therefore a small rectangle with a darker flue inside it, never a tower with sides. WEATHERED CEDAR SHINGLE SEEN FROM TEN METRES: shingles do not resolve individually, so the surface reads as faint COURSES running parallel to each ridge with a gentle mottling where some have weathered lighter. Never shingle by shingle, never a crisp grid. COLOUR: the roofs are a warm weathered grey around #9C968B, from #7B766C in the shaded slope to #B4AEA3 on the lit one, with the veranda band a shade darker than the main roof so the step reads. Eaves, ridge and the committee deck are picked out in clean white trim around #F5F5F3. THE BURGEE'S NAVY AND RED ARE THE ONLY SATURATED COLOURS IN THE PICTURE. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no terrace, no path, no dock, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The club stands alone on a transparent background. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no boat, no car, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing.
assets.note: THE FLEET'S HOME, and the only asset in the game that carries the SaltyCritter Yacht Club's own mark. The base prompt every asset in this library is built from opens 'Stylized polished 2D game art for SaltyCritter Yacht Club'; this is the first time the club appears as an object in the world rather than as a house style. Role LANDMARK — venue identity, on land, never an obstacle in the water. SIZE 168 units = 18.3m, deliberately between the boat shed (150) and the church (184): the church stays the largest building in the town, which is right for a New England harbour, and the club is the largest thing on the WATERFRONT after the marina. THE BURGEE IS THE ASSET AND THE PHYSICS ARE WHY IT WORKS. A flag flies HORIZONTALLY, so unlike the lighthouse's vertical lightning rod it does not collapse to a dot — you see the whole pennant from directly above. This is the same reasoning that made cove-church's weathervane succeed where the lighthouse's rod failed, and it is now the third asset in this venue to turn on the same question: STATE WHICH AXIS THE PART LIES ON AND THE ANSWER FOLLOWS. Vertical parts foreshorten to a dot (rod, chimney, flagpole, baluster); horizontal parts are seen whole (weathervane arrow, burgee). COLOURS COPIED FROM assets/images/misc/salty-crew-yacht-club-burgee.png, measured rather than eyeballed: navy #1C2E6E over 72k px, red #D83839 over 47k, white paw. Those two saturated hues appear nowhere else on this shore, which is deliberate — the club's flag should be the thing your eye finds. THE PENNANT IS DRAWN OVERSIZE at about a fifth of the building's length (~34 units), and that is a declared exaggeration in the scale block's sense: a real burgee on a real clubhouse pole would be a few pixels and would read as dirt. THE RAILING CLAUSE IS REUSED VERBATIM from cove-lighthouse and cove-house-captains, where it has now delivered twice — sixty correct balusters on the light's gallery and a clean widow's walk on the captain's house. Handrail as a line, balusters as end-on ticks. It is the most reliable sentence in this venue's whole prompt set and should be copied rather than rewritten. THE VERANDA IS THE SECOND CUE and it is the ell's valley applied to a wrap: a lower roof band stepped down from the main block, with a diagonal valley at each corner where it turns. cove-cottage-ell round 2 proved the generator can draw a valley when the geometry is stated in frame directions, so this asks for the same thing round a corner. If the veranda comes back as three separate awnings rather than one continuous band, that is the failure to watch for. PAIRS WELL WITH cove-parasol on the lawn and cove-marina in front of it — the club, its float and its boats are the one part of this waterfront that is about the regatta rather than about the working port. planRound false, allowSymmetry true (a gable roof is symmetric, the balusters are evenly spaced, the shingle courses are a 'tiled pattern' — the three reasons every building in this town needs it). PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °` so the veranda faces the water. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ REVISED AFTER ROUND 1 ON THREE COUNTS. (1) A CLUB NEEDS A DECK, and the first subject not only lacked one, it BANNED it ('no deck on the water') while asking for a wraparound veranda instead. The veranda was an invention; the deck is what a yacht club is. It is also the better top-down subject: a deck is OPEN TO THE SKY, so you see its FLOOR — pale planking beside a shingled roof, and every other building in this town is roof-only, so visible planking is the strongest 'this is a club' cue available. AND IT IS FURNISHED rather than left bare: four Adirondack chairs facing the water, two tables with chairs, two parasols. The bayou-dock 'leave it empty' rule does NOT apply here, and the reason is worth stating — that rule exists because a baked-in boat can only be placed once before it reads as a copy of itself, and there is exactly ONE yacht club in a venue. A single placement cannot repeat, so baking the furniture in costs nothing and buys the thing the building is FOR. (2) THE FLAGPOLE WAS DRAWN IN ELEVATION — a diagonal stick with a ball finial, a side view sitting in an otherwise-nadir image, and the same failure as the lighthouse's lightning rod. It now gets its own warning clause: a vertical pole IS A SMALL CIRCLE from above, and the burgee is visible only because a flag lies FLAT. That contrast — pole invisible, flag whole — is the clearest statement of the axis rule this venue has produced. (3) THE BURGEE CAME BACK WRONG IN THREE MEASURABLE WAYS. Measured against the club's own burgee file: the real flag is 1.45:1, the delivery 2.15:1; the real red band covers 43% of the length running 24%-67% along, the delivery's 26% at 23%-49%, so it read as a thin stripe near the hoist rather than a broad central band; and the real outline tapers linearly to one point (100/75/50/25% of hoist height at each quarter) where the delivery had a wavy swallowtail. THE SWALLOWTAIL WAS THE SUBJECT'S OWN FAULT — it asked for 'a soft ripple along its trailing edges', which on a shape whose identity IS a clean straight taper is an instruction to destroy it. THE GENERAL LESSON, recurring across this venue: WHEN A SUBJECT HAS AN EXACT REFERENCE ON DISK, MEASURE IT AND QUOTE THE NUMBERS — 'about a third of the way along' loses to '24% to 67%, covering two fifths' every time. ⚠️ ROUND 2: THE FLAGPOLE IS GONE AND THE BURGEE IS NOW PAINTED ON THE ROOF. Round 2 came back with the deck exactly right — four Adirondack chairs in a row, two tables, two parasols, committee deck, chimney — and the flag apparatus wrong AGAIN: the pole drawn as a vertical stick with a ball at each end, and the pennant blown up to half the sprite. THE DIAGNOSIS IS THAT A FLAGPOLE IS THE WORST POSSIBLE SUBJECT FOR THIS CAMERA, and it is not a wording problem. Its entire identity is height; the plan view deletes all of it and leaves a dot; and every reference image in existence is side-on. That is the red cedar's problem, the lighthouse rod's problem and the church steeple's problem stacked on one object, and two escalating rewrites did not move it. THE FIX IS TO CHANGE WHAT THE OBJECT IS. A burgee PAINTED on the roof cannot fail the orthographic test, because paint on a flat surface is two-dimensional by construction — there is no height for the camera to lose and no side for it to show. It is also REAL (boathouses and hangars carry aerial markings), it makes the club's mark LARGE and legible where a flown burgee at true scale would be a few pixels, and it puts the game's own brand where every boat racing past can see it. THE GENERAL LESSON IS THE MOST USEFUL ONE THIS VENUE HAS PRODUCED: when a subject's identity IS its verticality, do not keep rewording the camera clause — REPLACE THE OBJECT WITH A FLAT ONE THAT CARRIES THE SAME MEANING. The alternative considered and rejected was a burgee weathervane on the ridge (too small to read, and the church already owns that device) and signal bunting along the deck rail (hangs vertically, so it foreshortens to dots — the same trap in miniature). ROUND 3 ACCEPTED, AND THE PAINTED BURGEE WORKED FIRST TIME. Measured against the club's own burgee file: the taper is now EXACT — 78 / 52 / 25 / 5 percent of hoist height at the quarter stations against a linear ideal of 75 / 50 / 25 / 5 — so the swallowtail and the ripple are gone and it is a clean isosceles triangle. ⚠️ THE ASPECT 'ERROR' IS NOT AN ERROR AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED'. The painted flag measures 2.03:1 against a reference of 1.45:1, and that is CORRECT PHYSICS: a marking painted on a PITCHED roof is foreshortened across the slope when seen from directly above, and 1.45 / cos(44deg) = 2.02. The delivery is exactly a 1.45:1 burgee lying on a 44-degree roof, which is a normal Cape pitch. Anyone re-measuring this later and 'correcting' the flag to 1.45:1 in plan would be drawing a burgee lying on a FLAT roof, which this building does not have. ONE GENUINE MISS, ACCEPTED: the red band came back 24% of the flag's length running 23-47% along, against a measured reference of 43% running 24-67% — so it reads as a narrower stripe than the real burgee. Band width is measured ALONG the length and is therefore NOT foreshortened, so unlike the aspect this one is real. It is invisible at race scale, where the paw is what carries the mark, so it ships. TONES 119 TO COVER 90%, well over the venue band of 16-46 and the highest of any bay building (church 37, marina 75, shop-row 76) — the cost of a deck full of furniture with its own soft shadows. Judged on the race-scale render rather than the number: at 168 units it reads clean and is the most identifiable building on the shore. Watch it if the deck ever gains more clutter.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE BUILDING, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over its roof — the picture a survey flight makes of a building. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE. No wall appears anywhere: no clapboard, no shingled siding, no window, no door, no porch, no step, no foundation, and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A NEW ENGLAND MEETING HOUSE — a white clapboard church, and after the light the tallest thing in the town. From above it is TWO PARTS JOINED. (1) THE NAVE: a long rectangle about 2:1 in plan under one straight ridge running its whole length, two equal slopes falling either side. (2) THE TOWER: a SQUARE block projecting from one gable end of the nave, narrower than the nave is wide, reading clearly as its own separate mass rather than as part of the roof. WHAT A ROOF IS FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE: flat slopes meeting along a RIDGE, the ridge a crisp straight line and the slopes either side FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES — one lit, one in shade, with a hard edge between them. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE. The roof OVERHANGS the walls below it, so the building's outline is the roof's own edge, finished with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all the way round. THE STEEPLE IS THE IDENTITY AND IT IS THE HARDEST PART OF THIS PICTURE. On top of the tower stands a tall slender SPIRE, and its whole height runs straight into the camera and disappears. FROM DIRECTLY OVERHEAD A SPIRE IS A SQUARE PYRAMID SEEN FROM ABOVE: a square with four crisp seams running from its corners in to a single point at the exact centre, its four faces at four slightly different tones. It is never a cone lying across the frame, never a tower with visible sides, never a triangle, and never a spike. AT THE APEX, A WEATHERVANE — and unlike a lightning rod this one IS visible from above, because a weathervane's arrow lies HORIZONTALLY. Draw it as a small flat dark silhouette crossing the spire's point: a slim pointer one way, a tail the other, lying flat on the picture. The mast it turns on is vertical and foreshortens to a single dot at the centre beneath it. COLOUR, AND THE CONTRAST IS THE WHOLE SIGNATURE. The nave's roof is a dark cool SLATE around #58606A, from #474E57 in shade to #6E7681 on the lit slope, its eaves and ridge lined in crisp white trim around #F5F5F3. THE TOWER AND THE SPIRE ARE WHITE — painted clapboard around #F5F5F3, shading no darker than #DCDCD8 on their shaded faces. A dark nave with a bright white tower standing at one end of it is what says CHURCH at a distance, and it is the only place in this town where two parts of one building are opposite in value. Keep both clean: no third hue anywhere on it. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no path, no drive, no yard, no fence, no wall, no hedge, no tree, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The building stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it is built on. NOTHING MODERN AND NOTHING ALIVE: no car, no person, no washing line, no solar panel, no aerial, no satellite dish, no roof vent beyond what is described here. THE BUILDING DOES NOT FILL THE PICTURE. Draw it at the plan proportion stated above and leave empty background around it on all four sides. Do NOT stretch, widen or lengthen it to reach the edges of the frame — the frame's shape says nothing about the building's shape, and a house pulled out to span a wide picture is the wrong building.
assets.note: The town's landmark and its largest building: a 20m nave = 184 units, bigger than the lighthouse (84) and second in the venue only to the two bridges. Role LANDMARK rather than ambient — with the light it is one of the two things that anchor the eye on this shore. THE WHITE CHURCH PROBLEM, AND ITS SOLUTION. A New England church is identified by being WHITE, and its whiteness lives in the walls — which are invisible in plan. What survives the camera is the roof, so the subject moves the identity onto the two parts that are genuinely white from above: the TOWER and the SPIRE, both painted clapboard, set against a dark slate nave. Dark long mass + bright square tower at one end is a silhouette nothing else here has, and it works at race scale where a steeple's height cannot. THE WEATHERVANE IS A DELIBERATE CONTRAST WITH THE LIGHTHOUSE and worth keeping straight: the light's lightning rod is VERTICAL, so it foreshortens to a dot and the subject bans drawing it as a line — the delivered art got that wrong and it is the light's one recorded defect. A weathervane's arrow is HORIZONTAL, so here the line is correct and the DOT is only the mast beneath it. Same physics, opposite answer; state which axis the part lies on and the rest follows. ⚠️ THE SPIRE IS THE FOURTH ASSET IN THIS VENUE TO NEED THE VERTICAL-FORESHORTENING SENTENCE (lighthouse rod, chimney stubs, dormer roofs, now this). That threshold was called in cove-cottage-saltbox's note: it now belongs in the shared ORTHO clause in prompt.py rather than being retyped per subject. Part of Lighthouse Cove's TOWN SET; see cove-cottage for the shared reasoning — why only roof outline, ridge, tone, furniture and size can carry variety from directly above, why allowSymmetry is REQUIRED on every building (ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE bans 'symmetrical arrangement', 'evenly spaced' and 'tiled pattern', all three of which a roof needs), and the planRound-false wording gap that each subject works around by stating its own plan proportion. Role ambient unless noted, plane surface, contact none. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °` per building. THE TOWN'S ROOFS ARE THREE MATERIAL FAMILIES, TIGHT WITHIN AND CLEAR BETWEEN, which is deliberate and is the opposite of forcing seven distinct tones: CEDAR SHINGLE (saltbox #b4aea3 L*71, cottage #9c968b L*62, captain's #8d8578 L*56) sits only 6-9 dE apart inside the family, because on the real Cape almost every roof is the same weathered cedar and a paint-chip ladder would read as seven unrelated buildings rather than one town; SLATE (ell #646c73 L*45, church #58606a L*40) is the cool formal pair; WORKING DARK (boatshed #6b6154 L*42, shanty #4a4744 L*30) is tar and creosote. Between families the separation is 13-16 dE. Form and size carry the distinction inside a family — a hipped roof at 129 does not need a different grey from a gable at 80 to be told apart. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ THE 2026-08-10 BUILDING BATCH CAME BACK STRETCHED TO THE CANVAS, and it is one systemic cause rather than three separate failures. Measured across the three deliveries: subject plan ratios of 1.90, 2.04 and 1.88 against requested 1.33, 1.25 and 1.20 — i.e. all three landed on the generation canvas's own 1.83 aspect, each filling 81-94% of BOTH canvas dimensions. The generator fills the frame it is given, and a requested proportion loses to the frame's shape every time. TWO FIXES, both applied: a `gen` field on every building slot so the operator asks for a SQUARE frame (or a 3:2 one for the church and boat shed, which really are long), and a clause in each subject saying the building must not be stretched to reach the edges. This is why the bridges carry `gen: 1024x3072` — the field already existed for exactly this and the town slots simply did not use it. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED, AND THE WEATHERVANE IS THE RESULT WORTH KEEPING. It came back exactly as specified: a flat horizontal arrow lying across the spire's point with the mast collapsed to a dot beneath it — the deliberate inverse of the lighthouse's vertical rod, which the lighthouse delivery got WRONG. Same generator, same venue, one clause apart: the difference is that this subject named which AXIS the part lies on and derived the answer from it. That is the formulation to reuse. The spire also arrived as a true square pyramid with four converging seams, and the dark-nave / white-tower contrast reads at race scale, which was the whole bet on how to make a white church legible from above.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TIMBER PILING, shot straight down from directly overhead. A piling is a post driven into the harbour bottom, and IT POINTS AT THE CAMERA, so its whole height runs into the lens and disappears. WHAT IS LEFT IS A CIRCLE: the sawn top of the pile, seen flat. NO LENGTH OF POST IS VISIBLE ANYWHERE — no side, no shaft, no barnacled flank running away from you, nothing that tells you the thing is tall. A post drawn with a visible side is a post drawn from the side, and it is wrong. WHAT YOU SEE, from the middle outward: (1) the SAWN END GRAIN, a disc of weathered timber with faint growth rings and one or two dark CHECKS — the radial splits an old pile always has — running from near the centre out to the rim; (2) a slightly PALER, ROUNDED-OFF RIM where decades of rain and sun have worn the sharp edge away; (3) a narrow IRON BAND just below that rim, a thin dark ring of rusted strap, broken and pitted rather than clean. The timber is a driftwood grey-brown around #7A6E5E, silvered to about #9C9182 on the crown and dropping to #4A4238 inside the checks. The iron is a dull rust brown around #6B4A38. IT IS ONE PILE, ALONE — not a cluster, not a pair, not a dolphin of three lashed together, and not a row. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: THE SMALLEST PROP IN THE VENUE AND THE MOST USEFUL PER GENERATION: it edges a berth, marks a ruined wharf, breaks up a rock shore, and gives the pelicans venues.md promises somewhere to sit. ⚠️ SIZE IS AN EXPLICIT EXAGGERATION AND THE SCALE BLOCK REQUIRES THAT BE DECLARED. A real harbour pile is 0.3-0.6m across, which at 9.2 units/m is 3-5px — at or below the floor where anything resolves at all (the same finding the penguin note records: a 0.5m footprint 'cannot carry a silhouette'). world 14 is 1.5m, roughly 3.3x life size. It is drawn big so that ONE of them is visible; that is the deliberate trade. SINGLE, NOT A CLUSTER, AND THAT WAS A CORRECTION. The first plan was a baked cluster of four or five, which is wrong twice over: a fixed arrangement stamps the same pattern at every placement, and a cluster cannot make a LINE along a wharf face. The editor already solves this better — addProps' comment reads 'ONE DRAG LAYS A STAND', scattering `count` props inside a dragged circle each with its own size and heading — so a stand of pilings is a gesture, not an asset. THIS IS THE ONE WATERFRONT PIECE TO PLACE WITH prop-spin ON: a sawn pile top has no front, and rotation variety is what stops a row reading as a stamp. planRound TRUE and allowSymmetry TRUE: a pile top genuinely IS a circle in plan, so the roundness test is the right tilt check and the radial-symmetry negatives would fight the subject. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. Aspect 1.080 inside the 1.12 planRound gate, silhouette-vs-circle IoU 0.944 so it is a clean disc, tones 41 in band, colour #7d7063 against a #7A6E5E spec. Growth rings and four radial checks all arrived. TWO THINGS RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED. A faint SKIRT of the post's side shows below the disc — 1.41% of the sprite — which is the one thing the subject banned; at world 14 that is 0.2px and invisible, so it ships. And ALL THE DETAIL IS LOST AT RACE SCALE: at 14px this is a brown dot. That is not a fault, it is the trade the size argument already declared — the asset does its work in GROUPS, and a row of eight reads unmistakably as a line of posts while a scatter of ten reads as a stand. Checked both before accepting. Resolution 0.05x is the lowest in the venue by far and entirely expected for a 14-unit prop off a 1024 master.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SECTION OF DRY-STONE WALL, shot straight down from directly overhead — the low fieldstone wall that runs between every pasture and lane on Nantucket and the Cape. ⚠️ THE PICTURE ITSELF IS A TALL NARROW STRIP — five times taller than it is wide — and the wall FILLS IT EDGE TO EDGE. Generate on a tall narrow canvas; a wide or square frame will produce a wall five times too thick, which is the one thing that cannot be corrected afterwards. THE WALL RUNS UP THE FRAME, a long straight narrow band about FIVE times as long as it is wide, running off the top edge and off the bottom edge. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for the whole length, nothing tapers or converges, and no side face is visible: a wall is a low thing and you are looking at its TOP. IT IS BUILT OF LOOSE STONES AND NOTHING ELSE — no mortar, no cement, no joint filler, no rendering. What you see from above is the TOP COURSE: a packed run of individual FIELDSTONES, each an irregular rounded lump of granite two or three of which span the wall's width, all of them different sizes and shapes, fitted together with narrow dark gaps where they do not quite meet. The stones are ROUNDED AND WORN, not quarried or squared — glacial cobbles picked out of a field — and they sit at slightly different heights, so each carries its own small hard-edged shadow onto its neighbour. A few larger stones stand out from the rest, and here and there a small one is wedged into a gap. ⚠️ THIS SECTION IS LAID END TO END WITH COPIES OF ITSELF TO MAKE A LONGER WALL, so BOTH SHORT ENDS MUST BE PLAIN AND SQUARE-CUT: the run of stones continues straight off both the top and the bottom edge of the picture, mid-stone, with no end cap, no finished terminal, no gatepost, no corner and no dark outline closing the wall off. The two long sides keep their outline; the two ENDS must not have one, or two sections butted together will show a double dark line at the join. NOTHING GROWS ON IT AND NOTHING LEANS ON IT: no moss, no lichen patch, no grass tuft, no bramble, no flower, no gate, no post, no rail, no wire. COLOUR: weathered granite fieldstone in a soft warm grey around #9A9287, from #6E695F in the gaps and shadows to #B8B1A4 on the sunlit tops, with one or two stones a shade warmer or cooler than the rest. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no grass, no lane, no soil, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The wall stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it runs across.
assets.note: The other half of the 'walls and lanes' answer, and it goes the OPPOSITE way to the lane: a wall is a PROP, not a ground. The reason is width. A lane is metres across and reads as a surface, so a polygon painted with a texture is exactly right; a dry-stone wall is about 0.9m across — 8 units — and a shape that thin would be almost entirely the coastline STROKE that drawIslands paints round every land polygon, with the body invisible between. The shape machinery is built for islands and a wall is not one. SIZE 150 units = 16.3m per section, chosen to keep placements manageable: a 100m field boundary is six drops rather than twenty. Sections butt end to end along a boundary and can turn a corner simply by butting at an angle — a dry-stone wall has no mitred joints, so there is no corner asset to draw. ⚠️ IT IS THE SECOND TILING PROP IN THE LIBRARY, AFTER cove-quay, AND IT INHERITS THAT ASSET'S HARD-WON LESSON: the house style puts a continuous dark contour round every prop, which is correct for a discrete object and FATAL at a butt joint — round 1 of the quay produced a double dark line down every join. So the subject asks for the outline on the two long sides ONLY and explicitly forbids it on the two ends, with the stone run continuing mid-stone off both edges. Check it the way the quay was checked: lay two copies end to end BEFORE anything else. The quay also proved the second half of this — state the required features FIRST and constrain their position second, never lead with a blanket prohibition, which is what deleted the quay's bollards in round 1. COLOUR DELIBERATELY SHARES THE coastalrock FAMILY (#9A9287 against the ground's #a19481, dE ~5) and that is not a collision to fix: a Nantucket wall IS built of the same glacial granite as the shore it stands above, and forcing it to a different grey would be the mistake the cedar-roof family note warns about. What matters is that it separates from the ground it is actually drawn ON — coastal scrub — where it clears comfortably. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none: it stands inland where no boat can reach. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °` per section. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET. ⚠️ ROUND 1: THE STONEWORK AND THE OPEN ENDS ARE RIGHT, THE PROPORTION IS NOT, AND THE CAUSE IS THE CANVAS. THE GOOD HALF FIRST, because it is the part that was hard: the ends came back GENUINELY OPEN — measured end drop 7 luma against internal stone-gap drops of 21, i.e. no closing contour, stones cut mid-stone at both edges. That makes this the FIRST TILING PROP IN THE LIBRARY to solve the problem cove-quay needed three rounds for and still only half-solved, and the wording that did it is worth copying: give the outline to the two long sides ONLY and say the stone run continues off both ends. Tones 47, colour in family. THE BAD HALF: ratio 1.70:1 against the 8:1 asked, which at world 150 is a wall 9.6m thick, and it cannot be cropped narrower without slicing stones down the long sides. ⚠️ THE PROPORTION LEVER IS THE FRAME, NOT THE SUBJECT, AND THIS VENUE HAS NOW PROVEN IT FIVE TIMES: quay asked 3.0 got 2.13, pier asked 4.0 got 2.57, boat shed asked 2.5 got 2.15, ferry asked 2.33 got 1.94, shop row asked 2.5 got 2.06. The generator converges on 2-2.6:1 whatever the words say, because it fills the canvas it is given — and every one of those arrived on the same 2816x1536. A `gen` field was already set here (1024x3072) and did not reach the generator. So the fix is not more insistent wording: it is GENERATING ON A TALL NARROW CANVAS. gen changed to 512x2560 and the frame's own shape is now stated in the FIRST LINE of the subject rather than left to the operator header, on the theory that a generator which reads the subject may at least argue with its own frame. Target lowered 8:1 -> 5:1 to be reachable; at world 150 that is a wall 30 units = 3.3m wide, which is 3.6x a real 0.9m dry-stone wall and is a DECLARED exaggeration of the same order as cove-piling's 3.3x — a true-width wall would be 8 units and invisible. ROUND 2 ACCEPTED, AND IT IS THE LIBRARY'S FIRST GENUINELY SEAMLESS TILING PROP. Ratio 6.32:1 against the 5:1 asked (round 1 was 1.70), ends still open — end drop 4 luma against internal stone-gap drops of 52 — tones 26, and at world 150 the wall draws 24 units = 2.6m thick, only 2.9x a real dry-stone wall, less exaggeration than budgeted. Verified by placing three sections at exactly `world` spacing and a fourth rotated 90 degrees: one continuous wall, no visible join, and the corner butts clean. THE ONLY THING THAT CHANGED WAS THE CANVAS. Round 1's subject already said 'eight times as long as it is wide' and delivered 1.70; round 2 said five and delivered 6.32 — because it was generated on a 512x2560 frame instead of the usual 2816x1536. That closes the five-asset pattern this venue documented (quay 3.0->2.13, pier 4.0->2.57, boat shed 2.5->2.15, ferry 2.33->1.94, shop row 2.5->2.06): THE FRAME IS THE PROPORTION LEVER AND THE SUBJECT IS NOT. Set `gen` and actually generate at it. ⚠️ fillTo IS 1.0, NOT THE LIBRARY'S USUAL 0.86, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. fillTo insets content inside the frame while drawProps draws the sprite at `world` px, so at 0.86 a 150-unit section would show only 129 units of wall and every butt joint would gap by 14%. At 1.0 the wall spans the frame exactly and sections butt at exactly `world`. THE INGEST MARGIN WARNING IS EXPECTED AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED': 'content reaches within 6% of the edge' is precisely what a tiling piece requires, and the 8% rotation margin the class asks for does not apply to a prop that is never rotated off its own axis. ⚠️ THIS ARITHMETIC ALSO APPLIES TO cove-quay, which shipped at fillTo 0.86: its deck spans 172 of its 200 units, so quay sections must be placed 172 apart, not 200. Left as-is rather than re-ingested, because changing it would move an asset that is already placed-ready; the spacing is recorded on the kind instead.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SMALL WOODEN TENDER, shot straight down from directly overhead — a harbour dinghy of the kind rowed out to a moored yacht. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. The BOW is at the top of the frame, narrow and pointed; the STERN is at the bottom, cut off square as a flat TRANSOM. The hull is about two and a half times as long as it is wide, widest a little aft of the middle, and its two sides curve symmetrically about the centreline. YOU ARE LOOKING DOWN INTO AN OPEN BOAT, and that is what separates it from every other hull in this venue: there is no deck and no cabin, so you see the INSIDE. Draw, from bow to stern: the small triangular foredeck at the bow; two or three THWARTS, plain plank seats running straight across the boat at even spacing; the FLOORBOARDS between them, a run of narrow boards along the bottom; and a pair of OARS stowed fore-and-aft along the inside of one side, their blades overlapping the foredeck. The inside is a shade lighter than the outside because it catches the sky. AROUND THE OUTSIDE, a narrow GUNWALE rail runs the whole way round as a clean unbroken band, a little paler than the hull, with a soft dark line of shadow inside it. A short length of pale mooring line lies coiled in the bow. COLOUR: a workboat hull in soft weathered white around #E4E1D8 outside, the interior bare varnished timber around #B8A077 with the thwarts a shade darker, and a single narrow accent stripe along the gunwale in the harbour's own deep green around #2E5E3A. Nothing bright, nothing new, nothing glossy. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The only new HULL in the waterfront set, and it earns that because it is below the venue's current floor: the bay already registers motorboat 48, tugboat 76, trawler 140 and both ferries, all `motion: fixed` and therefore already placeable as moored scenery, so nothing above ~45 units needed drawing. A harbour also needs craft too small to be traffic, and 30 units = 3.3m is a tender. ROLE ambient, NOT traffic, and the distinction is art-pipeline 2's: `traffic` carries a contract about never being confusable with a competitor, which matters for a vessel underway. This one is furniture at a mooring or hauled up a beach. THE OPEN INTERIOR IS THE ASSET. Every other hull in this venue is decked, so a boat you can see the thwarts and floorboards inside is instantly a different class of object at race scale, where a 30px shape has no room for anything subtler. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. THE HULL FORM IS RIGHT AND IT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN EYEBALLED — a first look read the stern as rounded, and the stations disprove it: the bow tip is 10% of max beam and the stern ends at 69%, so the transom is genuinely broad and square, and the widest station is at 60% down, exactly the 'a little aft of the middle' the subject asked for. Ratio 2.09:1 against 2.5, inside the honest range for a tender. Green gunwale stripe present at 4% of the sprite, oars stowed both sides, three thwarts, floorboards, coiled painter in the bow, real alpha. ⚠️ TONES 93, DOUBLE THE VENUE BAND, ON A 30-UNIT SPRITE — and that is accepted rather than a fault, because of what survives the reduction. At 30px none of the interior detail resolves; what does is the thing that identifies the asset, a WARM OPEN INTERIOR inside a PALE GUNWALE, where every other hull in this venue is a closed deck. Checked on the race-scale render beside cove-motorboat (48, white and decked) before accepting. Resolution 0.12x is the second-lowest in the venue after the piling and is expected for a 30-unit prop off a 1024 master; the master is archived at full detail if it is ever wanted larger.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A TIMBER WHARF FINGER, shot straight down from directly overhead — a working town pier standing on piles. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE DECK IS THE PICTURE: heavy timber planks laid ACROSS the width, board by board, running the whole length. Several boards are visibly paler or darker than their neighbours from weathering, and the plank lines are the only rhythm in the image — they run at RIGHT ANGLES to the pier's length, never along it. PILING HEADS STUD BOTH LONG EDGES at even intervals, six or seven a side, each one a dark circle of sawn end grain standing slightly proud of the deck with a hard shadow on the boards beside it. They are seen END-ON from above and are never posts with visible sides. Two or three BOLLARDS stand on the deck near the outer end — squat dark cylinders, also circles from above, thicker than the pilings. A few coils of mooring line lie flat on the boards. THIS PIER IS IN USE AND SOUND: no missing boards, no gaps, no collapse, no rot holes, no derelict leaning. COLOUR: weathered timber decking around #8B7B63, from #6A5C48 in the shaded plank gaps to #A89A80 on the sun-bleached boards. Pilings and bollards are a darker creosoted brown-black around #4A4038. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The repeatable town wharf, and the piece a designer places most. SIZE: 150 units = 16.3m, chosen against bayou-dock's reasoning — 'long enough to pinch a lane, short enough that sailing past it is a decision rather than a wall' — scaled up for a commercial harbour rather than a bayou landing. TWO PLACED AT NINETY DEGREES MAKE AN L OR A T-HEAD and three in a row make a quay, which is why there is no separate pier-head asset: the variety is in the arrangement, not in more sprites. NO BOAT IS DRAWN ON IT, and that is bayou-dock's rule for the same reason: a boat baked into the sprite can only be placed once before it reads as a copy of itself, and the bay already has five hulls that can be parked alongside. PLANK DIRECTION IS LOAD-BEARING — across the width, never along the length. It is the same trick the boat shed uses to separate board from shingle, and here it is what stops a pier reading as a plain bar at race scale. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. The plank direction — the cheap differentiator this asset leans on — came back correct: vertical luma gradient 5.04 against horizontal 2.99, so the boards run ACROSS the width as a pier is decked, not along it. Real alpha, runs up the frame, pilings studding both long edges, bollards and rope coils at the outer end, shore platform at the root, no missing boards. TWO DEVIATIONS ACCEPTED. Ratio came back 2.57:1 against the 4:1 asked, so it reads as a landing rather than a long wharf; that is what the repeat-it design is for, and two placed end to end give the length. And the PILING HEADS ARE DRAWN AS LITTLE CYLINDERS WITH VISIBLE SIDES rather than the flat sawn discs cove-piling delivered — the same ortho slip as the lighthouse finial, at about 10px on a 150-unit sprite, so invisible in play. Worth knowing the standalone cove-piling got this RIGHT while the pier's did not: a small object drawn alone gets the camera clause's full attention, and the same object drawn twelve times as furniture on a bigger subject does not.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SECTION OF SOLID CARGO QUAY, shot straight down from directly overhead — the built-up concrete edge a freighter ties against, not a timber pier on piles. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. Everything interesting lives in the middle. THE DECK is poured concrete, a broad flat grey surface divided by straight EXPANSION JOINTS running across the width at even intervals, with patches where the concrete has been repaired in a slightly different tone and dark oil staining near the edge. Along the SEAWARD long edge — the top edge of the picture — runs a heavy dark COPING BAND, and hanging just outside it a row of FENDER TIMBERS: thick vertical baulks seen end-on from above as a line of short dark rectangles at even spacing. BOLLARDS: three heavy cast-iron mooring bollards spaced along the seaward edge, each a squat dark circle with a wider foot flange, far bigger than a pier bollard. Between them, two flush mooring RINGS set into the coping. COLOUR: weathered concrete around #9A968E, from #7B776F in the joints and stains to #B4B0A6 on clean slabs. The coping and fenders are dark creosoted timber near #46403A, the bollards a rusted cast iron near #5B4A40. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The freight side's substrate, and NOT cove-pier resized. A pier is a timber finger reaching OUT on piles; a quay is a solid edge the land is built up to, with a hard vertical face. Different structure, different material, different silhouette at race scale — a broad pale concrete band against a narrow dark timber one. SIZE: 200 units = 21.7m. Lay three or four for a 65-87m berth, which is what the 720-unit (78m) cargo ship actually needs; one 700-unit monolith would be the largest sprite in the game and could only make one length of quay. ⚠️ THE TILING REQUIREMENT IS UNIQUE TO THIS ASSET IN THE WHOLE LIBRARY and is why the ends are specified so hard. Every other prop is placed as a discrete object; this one is designed to butt against copies of itself, so a bollard or a ladder near an end would repeat at a countable interval — the same failure the texture class guards against with 'no feature deliberately centred', arriving here on a prop. Check the ends on delivery by laying two copies side by side before anything else. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 2 ACCEPTED, AND THE TILING IS FIXED — which was the hard part and the whole reason this asset was risky. Measured end-to-end difference fell from 47.9 luma in round 1 to 21.1, and butted the join now reads as another slab joint rather than as a seam; round 1 produced a double dark line because the house-style contour ran round all four sides. THE FURNITURE ALSO CAME BACK — three bollards, two mooring rings and the fender row — which round 1 lost entirely. THE CAUSE OF THAT LOSS IS THE REUSABLE LESSON: round 1 led with a blanket prohibition ('no bollard, no ladder, no marking and no feature of any kind within a hand's width of either end'), and read as a global instruction rather than a positional one it deleted the furniture everywhere. Round 2 leads with the furniture as required and states the end rule as a constraint on WHERE those items sit. State what you want first; constrain its position second. ⚠️ ONE DEVIATION ACCEPTED AND IT IS A REAL ONE: the deck came back COOL BLUE-GREY at hue 199 deg and L* ~33 against a spec of warm weathered concrete #9A968E (hue ~36 deg, L* ~62) — much darker and much cooler than asked. Accepted because it happens to serve the design rather than fight it: at L* 33 it separates hard from the shipped coastalrock ground (#a19481, L* 60), so it reads as BUILT rather than as a natural ledge, and a cool dark working quay against the town's warm shingle-and-hydrangea shore is exactly the two-waterfront contrast the freight side was added to create. If a warm concrete is wanted later, reroll COLOUR ONLY and keep everything else — the tiling took two rounds to get and is the expensive part. ROUND 3 REPLACES ROUND 2 ON DISK, better on both counts that were wrong. COLOUR came back WARM at hue 42 deg — the weathered concrete the subject always asked for — against round 2's cool blue-grey 199 deg. TILING improved again: end-to-end difference 47.9 (r1) -> 21.1 (r2) -> 11.8 (r3), and the furniture is all present. Tones 29, the cleanest of the waterfront set. ⚠️ THE JOIN STILL SHOWS A LINE, AND THE METRIC I USED HIDES IT — worth recording because it is a flaw in the TEST, not just the art. Measuring 'do the two ends match' rewards a sprite whose ends both carry the house contour: they match perfectly and butting them DOUBLES the dark line. The right test is 'does the end have a contour at all'. Accepted anyway because the quay's own expansion joints drop 44 luma, so a doubled contour lands in the same range and reads as a heavy joint rather than a foreign seam — and this asset legitimately has vertical joints every few metres. A truly seamless quay needs the outline suppressed on the two short ends, which fights the house style; the standing alternative is to make the deck a bay-concrete TEXTURE and the furniture separate props, exactly as bay-lane does for lanes. DELIVERED OPAQUE ON WHITE and cut here with a border-flood key on the near-white AND unsaturated test, which kept 0 enclosed pale slabs — the bayou-oak method, and the reason a plain luminance threshold was not used.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL FERRY TERMINAL, shot straight down from directly overhead. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. It is a broad rectangular APRON running up the frame, about two and a third times as long as it is wide — noticeably WIDER than a timber pier, because vehicles turn on it. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE DECK is heavy timber planking laid ACROSS the width over most of its length, with the landward third surfaced in dark asphalt instead and a pale broken line painted down its middle where the vehicle lane runs. Where the two surfaces meet there is a straight hard edge. AT THE TOP OF THE FRAME, THE WATER END, IS THE THING THAT MAKES THIS A FERRY BERTH AND NOT A PIER: a hinged VEHICLE TRANSFER RAMP projecting straight out beyond the apron — a rectangular steel deck, narrower than the apron, with a clear straight HINGE LINE across its root where it pivots, ribbed with cross-members along its length, and a blunt square lip at its far end. It is a step lower than the apron and reads as a separate plate. FLANKING THE BERTH, two MOORING DOLPHINS stand off the apron in the water, one either side near the top — each a tight bundle of piles bound with an iron band, seen from above as a small cluster of dark circles with a walkway of two planks reaching back to the apron. They are what a ferry noses between. Along both long edges, a run of heavy FENDER TIMBERS seen end-on as short dark rectangles, and four BOLLARDS on the apron. A small square TICKET SHELTER stands on the landward third, off to one side of the vehicle lane: a plain flat-roofed box, its roof a pale grey panel with a dark rim. COLOUR: timber decking around #8B7B63, asphalt near #4E4A46 with #D8D3C4 lane paint, the steel ramp a cool grey-blue near #6E747C, dolphins and fenders creosote near #46403A. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The berth for cove-ferry (300 units) and cove-fast-ferry (200), and it exists as its own asset rather than as a longer cove-pier because a ferry terminal has three things a wharf does not: a vehicle apron wide enough to turn on, a hinged transfer ramp, and dolphins to guide the hull in. SIZE: 320 units = 34.8m, giving a berth face slightly longer than the ferry itself. THE RAMP IS THE IDENTITY AND THE HINGE LINE IS WHAT SELLS IT. From directly above a ramp and a pier extension are the same rectangle; the hinge is the one mark that says the plate moves. If the delivery returns a plain projecting deck with no hinge line, it has failed on the thing that distinguishes this asset from cove-pier. THE DOLPHINS ARE DRAWN IN rather than left to cove-piling placements, because their position relative to the ramp is the geometry of a berth and not a decorating choice. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. The ramp, the dolphins and the fender rows all arrived: steel-grey reads 39% of the sprite against 59% timber, the plank grain runs ACROSS the apron (horizontal gradient 5.34 vs vertical 2.29), and the mooring dolphins came back as clusters of small circles — piles seen correctly END-ON, which the pier's own piling heads did not manage. Ratio 1.94 against the 2.33 asked, and the asphalt vehicle lane and ticket shelter did not appear; both are accepted, since at 320 units the ramp and dolphins are what identify a ferry berth and they are unmistakable. Tones 66, in line with the marina (75) and shop row (76). ⚠️ BAKE LOWERED 4 -> 2, AND THIS IS THE FIRST BAY ASSET TO NEED IT. At world 320 the profile's 4x bake asks for 1280px from a master that holds 881px of content, so ingest reported 1.25x UPSCALED — 400px invented. The world-prop profile note is explicit that the fix is to lower `bake` rather than raise `world`, because bake is oversampling for device pixel ratio and the camera is 1:1: at this size the headroom was never going to be spent. 2x gives 640px and 0.62x resolution. The cove cargo family made the same trade for the same reason. ANY FUTURE BAY PROP ABOVE ~220 UNITS WILL HIT THIS — master/bake = 256 is the ceiling, so world 256 is where 4x stops being free.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL FLOATING MARINA, shot straight down from directly overhead — the slotted dock system a yacht club keeps its small craft in. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. THE SHAPE IS A COMB. One long MAIN WALKWAY runs up the frame, and off ONE side of it — the right — six narrow FINGER DOCKS project at right angles, parallel to each other and EVENLY SPACED along its length, with an open SLIP of water between each pair. All six fingers are the same length and the same width; the walkway is about twice as wide as a finger. This is a manufactured object and its regularity is correct: the fingers must be genuinely parallel and genuinely evenly spaced, not scattered. IT FLOATS, SO IT IS FLAT AND LOW. There are no piles, no legs and no height anywhere: what you see is DECKING, pale timber planks laid across the short axis of every walkway and finger. A dark RUBBING STRIP runs round the whole outline — walkway edges, finger sides, finger ends — as one continuous band, and it is the strongest line in the picture. ON THE DECK: a pair of small dark CLEATS at the outer end of each finger and two more along the walkway, each a flat double-ended horn; one small square DOCK BOX standing at the head of the walkway at the bottom of the frame, a plain low lid with a dark rim; and short lengths of chain running off two corners to the edge of the picture. THE SLIPS ARE EMPTY. No boat, no yacht, no dinghy, no mast, no mooring line strung across a slip — the gaps between the fingers are open transparent background and nothing is drawn in them. COLOUR: pale weathered decking around #C9BCA4, #A79879 in the plank shadows, #DCD2BC on newer boards; rubbing strip near-black #33302B; cleats galvanised grey #7E8288. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The single most placement-efficient asset in the venue: one drop gives six berths and a whole yacht-club frontage that would otherwise be a dozen hand-aligned props. SIZE: 240 units = 26m, a small club marina; fingers off ONE side only so that two placed back to back make a double, which is more flexible than baking both sides in. THE ONE CASE WHERE A COMPOSED GROUP BEATS SCATTERED PARTS, against art-pipeline 3b's default. That rule exists because image models return symmetric rosettes when asked for 'seven of X' and a rosette reads as a snowflake at race scale — but a marina IS a regular repeating array, so the failure mode the rule guards against is here the correct answer. allowSymmetry true is mandatory for the same reason: 'evenly spaced' and 'symmetrical arrangement' are exactly what is being asked for. CONTACT NONE, unlike the rest of the waterfront set, and it is the cargo-ship argument: a circle fits a slotted comb worse than it fits anything else here — sized to the outline it seals six slips of open water, sized smaller it stops nothing. A hidden shape per finger is available if a placement ever needs teeth. EMPTY SLIPS, per bayou-dock: the bay already has five hulls that can be parked in them, and a boat baked into the sprite can be placed exactly once. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED, AND THE REGULARITY IS MEASURED RATHER THAN EYEBALLED: six fingers, pitch 244/235/236/237/238 px — a 9px spread across five gaps, i.e. genuinely evenly spaced — all parallel, all the same length, slips open and empty. That is exactly what allowSymmetry was turned on for, and it vindicates the departure from art-pipeline 3b: the rule bans composed groups because models return rosettes, but a marina IS a regular array, so the attractor the rule guards against was the correct answer here. Delivered running UP the frame with the fingers to the right, so `world` 240 fits the long axis and the comb comes out 26m x 15m. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SHIP-TO-SHORE CARGO CRANE standing on a quay, shot straight down from directly overhead. ⚠️ THE PICTURE IS A WIDE HORIZONTAL STRIP, three times wider than it is tall, and the crane fills it end to end. THE BOOM RUNS LEFT-TO-RIGHT ACROSS THE FRAME — it points out over the water to the RIGHT, and the landward machinery and rails sit at the LEFT. Generate on a wide canvas. This matters more than it sounds: a crane drawn from the SIDE is a tall thing and cannot fit a wide strip, so the frame itself is what forces the correct view. ⚠️ A CRANE IS A TALL THING AND THIS PICTURE SHOWS NONE OF THAT HEIGHT. Every reference image of a cargo crane is taken from the ground or the sea, looking UP at a tower; this is the opposite, and it is the whole difficulty. From directly overhead there is NO TOWER, NO MAST, NO VERTICAL LATTICE and NO SILHOUETTE AGAINST THE SKY. A leg is not a column — it is a small SQUARE where it lands. The machinery house is not a box with faces — it is a flat RECTANGLE, its roof. Nothing tapers, nothing narrows toward any end, nothing recedes, and no part is drawn smaller for being further away, because every part is the SAME distance from the lens. ⚠️ THE SUREST TELL OF A WRONG PICTURE IS A LATTICE THAT NARROWS: a boom seen from above is the SAME WIDTH for its whole length, from the machinery house right out to its blunt tip. If the steelwork tapers, you have drawn a tower from the side. WHAT YOU SEE, from the right of the frame leftward: (1) THE BOOM, a long narrow steel LATTICE reaching out over the water to the RIGHT, of CONSTANT WIDTH end to end — drawn as two parallel main rails with a regular zig-zag of cross-bracing between them, the pattern unbroken along its whole length, ending in a blunt square head; (2) THE MACHINERY HOUSE where the boom meets the frame, a solid rectangular box with a flat panelled roof, the one closed mass in the picture; (3) THE PORTAL FRAME behind it, a broad open square of girders; (4) FOUR LEGS at the corners of that square, each seen END-ON as a small solid square where it lands, with a dark shadow beside it; and (5) TWO RAILS running TOP-TO-BOTTOM across the LEFT end of the frame, beneath the legs, a pair of straight parallel lines with sleepers between them, reaching a little way past the crane on both sides. A SPREADER hangs beneath the boom about two thirds of the way out: a plain rectangular frame, seen as a smaller oblong outline lying on the boom's line, with four corner blocks. COLOUR: painted industrial steel in a dull weathered RED-BROWN around #8E4536, from #6B3327 in shadow to #A9604F on lit surfaces, with the machinery house roof a cool grey #6E747C and the rails bare rust #7A5344. ⚠️ IT MUST NOT BE THE SUSPENSION BRIDGE'S ORANGE: that span is international orange #C0362C and this is browner, duller and darker, so the two never read as the same painted structure. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in.
assets.note: The freight side's identity, and the only LANDMARK in the waterfront set — role landmark rather than hazard because it stands ON the quay rather than reaching into the channel, which is exactly the line art-pipeline 2 draws ('a landmark never reads as an obstacle in the water'). SIZE: 230 units = 25m, a small ship-to-shore crane, tall in life and modest in plan. ⚠️ THE BOOM OVERHANGS THE WATER AND STRICTLY WANTS TO BE A SPLIT PAIR. It stands ~30m up, so a boat can pass beneath it — which by the plane rules makes the boom `canopy` and the legs `surface`, exactly the trunk/crown split the bayou trees carry. It ships as ONE `surface` sprite anyway, because in practice the berth beneath a working crane is occupied by the ship it is unloading, and paying for a split pair to serve a placement nobody will author is the wrong trade. This is the same coupling recorded on the shore trees: anyone re-planing this to `canopy` is changing what it occludes, and should split it first. THE LATTICE IS THE RISK. A generator asked for a crane from above will reach for a solid beam; the boom's identity is that it is OPEN steelwork, and the truss bridge's subject already proved the fix — describe it as a repeating zig-zag between two rails rather than as a 'lattice'. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ ROUND 1 CAME BACK AS A FRONT ELEVATION and the reroll changes the FRAME, not the wording, because the wording was already explicit. The delivery had the rails correct — two parallel lines with cross-ties, a true plan — and everything above them in side view: a lattice that NARROWS toward the top like a tower in perspective, portal legs showing their full vertical length, a machinery house drawn as a 3D box with faces, and no horizontal boom at all. Subject aspect 0.93, i.e. essentially square, which is the shape of a crane ELEVATION. THE FIX IS A WIDE FRAME AND IT IS A SHARPER VERSION OF THE WALL'S LESSON. The wall proved the frame sets the proportion; this goes further — a crane seen from the SIDE is a tall object and physically cannot fill a 3:1 wide strip, so the frame does not merely bias the proportion, it makes the wrong VIEW impossible. gen is now 3072x1024 with the boom running left-to-right and the frame's shape stated in the subject's first line. A NEW TELL WAS ADDED because it is the one thing that cannot be faked: a boom seen from above is the SAME WIDTH for its whole length, so a lattice that tapers is a tower drawn from the side. ⚠️ THIS BREAKS THE 'FRONT FACES THE TOP' CONVENTION deliberately — the boom points right at heading 0 rather than up — and the trade is worth it: a designer sets `heading` per placement anyway, and no heading can rescue a sprite drawn in elevation. Note it when registering the kind. bake set to 2 preemptively: at world 230 the profile's 4x would ask 920px of a master holding 881, which is the upscale the ferry hit.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A BLOCK OF SHIPPING CONTAINERS standing on a quay, shot straight down from directly overhead. A CONTAINER SEEN FROM ABOVE IS SIMPLY A RECTANGLE — this is the easiest subject in the venue and the only thing to get wrong is the camera. No side, no end, no door, no corrugated flank running away from you: you see the flat ROOF of each box and nothing else. THE BLOCK IS A TIGHT GRID: two rows of three or four containers, laid side by side with their long axes running UP the frame, packed with only a hand's width of gap between neighbours and the rows squared off against each other. Every container is the same size and they line up cleanly — this is a stacking yard and its regularity is correct. ON EACH ROOF: fine CORRUGATION ribs running ACROSS the short axis, evenly spaced the whole length; a small dark CORNER CASTING at each of the four corners; and on two or three of them a faint rectangular patch where the paint has been repaired. Two containers are STACKED — drawn as the same rectangle a touch larger with a hard dark shadow cast onto the box beside it, which is the only cue that they are two high. COLOUR IS THE WHOLE CHARM AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE IN THE TOWN THAT CARRIES SATURATION: give the block a mixed set — one rust red around #9B4032, one faded maritime blue around #35566E, one weathered sea green around #3D6B57, one dull grey around #7D8188, one bleached white-grey around #C4C1B8. Each container is ONE flat colour with a slightly darker tone in the corrugation shadows, all of them chalky and sun-faded, none of them glossy or new. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number. NO TEXT OF ANY KIND: no shipping line name, no lettering, no serial number, no logo, no placard.
assets.note: The cheapest readable asset in the venue by a wide margin, and the reason is worth stating: a container from directly overhead IS a rectangle, so this subject has no foreshortening trap, no vertical part to collapse to a dot, and no side-view prior to fight. Every other asset in this venue has spent its longest clause on the camera; this one does not need to. SIZE: 115 units = 12.5m, a block of six to eight boxes. IT IS ALSO THE VENUE'S COLOUR RELIEF. The whole town is grey, slate and cedar and the freight side is concrete and rusted steel; a mixed block of containers is the one place saturated colour belongs on this shore, and it reads at race scale when nothing else at 115 units would. allowSymmetry true because a stacking yard is a manufactured grid — 'evenly spaced' and 'tiled pattern' are precisely what is wanted. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED, AND IT WAS THE ONLY SUBJECT IN THE VENUE WITH NO CAMERA PROBLEM — exactly as the note predicted. A container from above IS a rectangle: no foreshortening trap, no vertical part to collapse, no side-view prior to fight, and the delivery came back a clean plan first try with corrugation ribs running across each box, corner castings at four corners, and a few stacked two high with hard shadows. Colour split rust 24% / green 22% / white-grey 20% / blue 18%, which is the mixed set asked for and the only saturated thing on the freight shore. ⚠️ WORLD RAISED 115 -> 225 AND THAT IS A SPEC CORRECTION, NOT A DELIVERY FAULT. The slot assumed a block two rows deep with the boxes' long axes running UP the frame — 12.2m long, hence 115. The delivery laid them the other way, four boxes end to end across the frame, which is 4 x 6.1 = 24.4m and needs world 224 for life size. At 115 each box would have drawn 3m long, obviously wrong beside a 78m cargo ship. Checked against the containers already painted on cove-cargo-ship's deck at race scale: the two now agree, which is the only scale test that matters for a freight yard. bake 3 rather than 4 because 225 x 4 = 900px would have asked more than the 881px the master holds — the ferry's lesson applied before ingest rather than after. Tones 154, the highest in the venue, and accepted for the same reason as the dinghy: at 225 units each box is ~56px, the ribs go sub-pixel, and what survives is a grid of flat coloured rectangles, which IS the asset.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL HARBOUR CAFE, shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE: no wall, no window, no door, no shopfront and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A SMALL RECTANGULAR BUILDING about 4:3 in plan. ⚠️ IT HAS A RIDGE AND THE RIDGE MUST READ: one straight line running left-to-right across the middle of the long axis, with the two slopes either side of it as FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES and a hard edge between them. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE, and a roof drawn as one uniform plane of shingles has failed. The roof overhangs the walls, so the outline is the roof's own edge with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all round. Its two long edges run parallel, nothing tapers, and no end wall is visible. ALONG THE LOWER LONG EDGE — the street side, at the bottom of the frame — an AWNING projects beyond the eaves: a straight strip of canvas in a deep harbour GREEN around #2E5E3A, about a sixth as deep as the building, its outer edge cut into a row of even scallops, with a hard shadow beneath its outer lip. It runs the full width.
