THE PREVIOUS DELIVERY WAS NOT A GENERATOR FAILURE. It was faithful to a brief that asked in as many words for an open crown with chalk-white limbs forking out of the middle, and it delivered exactly that at 42.9% fill and a 30.3% alpha harmonic. Seen alone it was the handsomest tree in the venue; seen four hundred at a time along a shore it read as WINTER. The lesson is recorded on [[lake-pine-white]]: species in one ambient role are seen in aggregate, so they must separate on SIZE and VALUE, never on silhouette novelty.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no stem, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. A BALSAM FIR — the dark, dense, perfectly conical little conifer that fills in under the pines all round a northern lake — AND IT IS A NARROW SPIRE, which is the whole difficulty of this picture. Every photograph of this tree ever taken is a tall pointed triangle seen from the SIDE, and FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE IT IS NOT TALL AT ALL: all of that height goes straight into the camera and disappears, and a spire seen from overhead is a SMALL, TIGHT, DENSE ROUND TUFT. Draw the tuft, not the spire. It is by far the SMALLEST and TIGHTEST crown of this venue's three trees — a compact closed rosette, where the white pine is a broad open raft of plates and the birch is an airy scatter of sprays. WHAT YOU SEE IS THE VIEW STRAIGHT DOWN A CONE. The centre is the TIP of the tree, its leading shoot: the nearest point to the camera and the brightest, a small pale crest of FOLIAGE at the middle — foliage, never a stem and never a hub. From there the needle-mass steps DOWN and OUTWARD in two or three flat rings, so the crown reads as a bright small core inside a distinctly darker skirt, with a CLEAN HARD EDGE between the steps and no soft gradient anywhere. THE NEEDLES ARE SHORT, FLAT AND DENSE, packed so tightly that the crown is CLOSED — you cannot see through it and there is nothing inside it to see. Its rim is finely bristled, a fine even fringe of short needle tips, and slightly ragged where a branch tip runs out further than its neighbours. Two or three shallow notches bite into the outline. It is irregular, but it is never a clean circle and never a star. COUNT NOTHING AND REPEAT NOTHING. Do not arrange the rim into evenly spaced points: walk around it, and if the same spacing comes back four, five or six times, it has been drawn as a snowflake and it is wrong. THIS IS THE DARKEST THING IN THE VENUE. A deep, cool, blue-green conifer: a lit tone near #235744 on the crest, a body near #173D31 through the skirt, and a shade near #0D261F in the notches. It must read plainly DARKER than the white pine beside it. NOTHING HERE IS OLIVE, KHAKI, YELLOW-GREEN, DUSTY OR GREY, and nothing is black — it is a saturated dark green, not an absence of colour. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. NO WATER ANYWHERE, and no ground is DRAWN
assets.note: THE VENUE'S SMALL DARK CONIFER, the one that fills in under the pines. Registered reasoning for the family is on [[lake-pine-white]]. SIZE IS HONEST: a balsam fir spreads about 6 m, and 6 x 9.2 = 55u. Bottom rung of the 110 / 80 / 55 ladder, and 2x under the white pine — which is the separation doing the real work, since the two are dE 8.8 apart in colour. ⚠️ THE SPIRE PROBLEM IS THE WHOLE SLOT, and it is solved by copying cove-cedar-red almost clause for clause, because that asset had exactly this difficulty and shipped. A narrow conical conifer is the one subject where the plan view destroys the silhouette the species is known by: all of its height is along the camera axis. The fix is to stop describing the tree and describe the PICTURE — a small tight tuft, a bright central crest that is the leading shoot, and two or three flat value steps going outward. State the failure too ('draw the tuft, not the spire'), because a generator will otherwise give you a side elevation. CLOSED, NOT OPEN, which is the one place it departs from its two siblings: the pine is asked for six tenths circle fill and the birch for a half, and this is asked to be solid. That is honest for a fir and it is also what makes the three separable at a glance with colour removed — open raft, open scatter, closed tuft. DARKEST IN THE VENUE at L* 22.8, so the forest floor sits +28.1 above it, lake sand +48.9 and gneiss +38.1 — the most comfortable margins of any plant here. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, NO allowSymmetry — the snowflake is this subject's specific failure mode and the arrangement negatives all apply. Plane `surface`, contact none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-15. Aspect 1.006 — the truest plan view of the batch — one connected mass, circle fill 85.0% against the 'closed, solid' the subject asked for, and mean #1B3F38 at dE 4.2 from spec, the closest colour match of the five. Halo +0.15. THE SPIRE PROBLEM WAS SOLVED: it came back as a small tight tuft with a bright central crest stepping outward into a darker skirt, which is what the cove-cedar-red clause asks for, and not as a side elevation. Darkest thing in the venue at L* 23.8, so the forest floor sits +19.8 above it at dE 37.5. ⚠️ ITS MIRROR CORRELATION IS 0.817, THE HIGHEST OF THE BATCH AND ABOVE THE ACCEPTED COVE OAK'S 0.696 — AND THAT IS NOT A DEFECT. The metric that catches a snowflake is the ANGULAR one, and this reads n=2 at 20.3%, well under the accepted 33%: there are no repeating spokes. What the mirror score is detecting is the CONCENTRIC construction the subject explicitly demanded — a bright core inside stepped rings — and concentric structure mirrors onto itself by definition. This refines the rule recorded on [[ocean-grass-coastal]]: the mirror test is the right check for BILATERAL fakery, but any compact concentric subject scores high on it honestly, so read it alongside the angular power rather than alone. ⚠️ THE CONIFER PAIR DRIFTED TEAL AND DID IT TOGETHER. Both this and its sibling came back at green-hue 169.7 against a spec of ~150 — a cyan-leaning green rather than the blue-green asked for. Accepted, on two grounds. It is CONSISTENT: the two are dE 8.7 apart, essentially the number the slots predicted (8.8), so the pair still reads as one genus and the separation work still falls on size and construction where it was designed to. And it suits the venue card, which commits to 'deep lake blue and pine green' — a teal conifer sits with that water rather than against it. If either is ever redrawn, redraw BOTH: the one thing that must not happen is one blue-green pine beside one teal one.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE SHRUB, shot straight down from well above it the way a survey frames a single plant. A SPECKLED ALDER — the multi-stemmed thicket shrub that rings every northern lake right at the waterline, standing in the wet ground between the beach and the forest. It is the TALLEST and LOOSEST of this venue's three underbrush plants. IT IS A THICKET, NOT A BUSH, and that is the construction. An alder throws several stems from one root rather than a single trunk, so from directly above you see THREE TO SIX SEPARATE LEAFY HEADS — one per stem — of plainly uneven size, leaning apart and overlapping where they meet, with real gaps of shadow between them. One head is clearly the largest. They do NOT sit in a ring around a centre; cluster them off to one side of each other so the whole plant leans. THE LEAF IS BROAD, OVAL AND COARSE — a rounded leaf with a bluntly toothed edge and a clearly marked midrib, noticeably bigger and coarser than anything else growing here. Draw them in loose overlapping groups of four to ten, each leaf a flat two-tone shape with a hard edge, so a head reads as a rough plate of separate leaves rather than a smooth mound. THE LITTLE WOODY CONES ARE THE IDENTIFIER. Alder carries small hard CONES — dark brown, the size of a thumbnail, egg-shaped and scaly — in tight bunches of three to five on short stalks at the ends of the stems. Show four to eight of them scattered across the plant, sitting on top of the leaves where the light gets to them. They are the only warm thing in the picture, and nothing else in this venue has them. THE GREEN IS A PLAIN, SLIGHTLY DULL MID GREEN — a wet-footed shrub, not a bright one. Build it from a lit tone near #56942C, a body near #386B1E and a deep shade near #1F4715 between the heads. It sits between the pale birch above it and the dark firs, and it must not be as bright as a fern. NOTHING HERE IS KHAKI, GREY-GREEN, DUSTY OR ARMY-DRAB — dull means unsaturated toward NOTHING, it means simply not brilliant. ONE CONNECTED PLANT: every head runs back to the same root and none floats free. Draw the smallest circle that contains it and the foliage fills about two thirds. The silhouette is as tall as it is wide. NO WATER ANYWHERE, and no ground is DRAWN — the shrub is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the shore it stands on
assets.note: STILLWATER LAKE'S SHORELINE SHRUB, and the one that makes a lake edge read as a lake edge rather than a beach. The underbrush set separates on silhouette first: this is a LOOSE MULTI-HEADED THICKET, [[lake-fern-bracken]] is a ROSETTE OF TRIANGULAR FRONDS, and [[lake-blueberry-lowbush]] is a LOW DENSE MOUND. Ladder 48 / 34 / 22 — 1.41x and 1.55x apart. All three stay under the balsam fir's 55u so the venue's shrub-under-tree ladder survives planting, the rule the ocean set follows too. SIZE IS HONEST: a speckled alder spreads about 5.2 m, and 5.2 x 9.2 = 48u. THE MULTI-HEAD CONSTRUCTION IS BORROWED DELIBERATELY FROM [[ocean-pandanus]], which used the same shape of clause and delivered it first time — three to six heads, uneven, clustered off-centre, one clearly largest. It is also the reason to expect the polar rosette metric to read high on delivery and to be WRONG about it: on the pandanus n=3 turned out to be the head count rather than a flower, and this will do the same. Judge it against the head count, or use the bilateral mirror test instead. THE CONES ARE WORTH THE PIXELS AT 48u because nothing else in the venue has a hard warm accent — the pine's cones are two or three, half-buried and slender; these are bunched, dark and sit proud. It is the cheapest identifier available at this size. COLOUR: L* 40.3, so the forest floor sits +10.6 above it — the tightest value margin of any plant in the venue, which is intentional, because an alder growing in the shade of a shore is genuinely a middling green. It still clears the ground at dE 37.8 because the separation is on HUE, not value. If a delivery comes back brighter than the fern it has taken the wrong rung and should be sent back. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, no allowSymmetry. Plane `surface`, contact none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-15. Aspect 1.020, ONE connected plant, circle fill 52.3% against the two thirds asked — looser, which suits a thicket. Mean #436229, dE 12.5 from spec, halo -0.09. THE CONES ARE THERE AND THEY ARE THE IDENTIFIER, in bunches on short stalks at the stem ends exactly as asked, at 7.4% warm pixels. The multi-head construction arrived too — three to four leafy heads of uneven size, leaning apart. ⚠️ ITS ROSETTE SCORE OF n=3 AT 40.8% IS THE HEAD COUNT, NOT A FLOWER, AND THE SLOT PREDICTED THIS. It is the only asset in the batch over the accepted cove oak's 33%, and the note above said in advance to expect it and why: [[ocean-pandanus]] scored n=3 for exactly the same reason, because a crown built from a small number of discrete heads has a genuine low-order angular component. The confirming measurement is the mirror test at 0.217 — one of the least self-similar sprites here — so there is no symmetry being faked. Judge a multi-headed subject against its head count, or use the mirror test instead. COLOUR SITS WHERE IT WAS ASKED TO, in the middle of the venue: L* 38.0, only 5.6 L* below the forest floor, which is the tightest value margin of any lake plant and is deliberate for a shade-grown shore shrub. It still clears the ground at dE 28.1 because the separation is on hue. It is also 18.7 from [[lake-aspen-quaking]] and 27.7 from the birch, so the three mid-and-light greens stay apart.

assets.subject: A PATCH OF BRACKEN FERN ON A FOREST FLOOR, photographed straight down from a metre or two above it. ⚠️ THE SUBJECT IS A PATCH, NOT A PLANT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE FIX. Three deliveries in a row came back as a single tidy fern rosette — six fronds, then eight, spaced evenly round one centre — because that is what a SINGLE bracken fern honestly looks like from directly overhead, and the brief kept asking for one. A lone fern seen from above IS a snowflake. So do not draw one. Bracken spreads underground and comes up in a dense colony, and what you are drawing is a piece of that mat: fifteen or twenty fronds belonging to DIFFERENT PLANTS whose roots are nowhere in this picture. THERE IS NO CENTRE. No point in this picture has more than two fronds meeting at it. The fronds lie at every angle with no common origin — some running left, some running down the frame, some diagonal — and their stems disappear under other fronds rather than converging anywhere. ⚠️ IF A VIEWER CAN COUNT THE ARMS, OR FIND THE MIDDLE, IT IS WRONG. ⚠️ THE CROSSINGS ARE THE PROOF, and they are the one thing a rosette cannot have. In at least four places one frond LIES ACROSS ANOTHER at a clear angle, the upper one throwing a soft dark shadow onto the lower. Fronds in a rosette radiate without ever overlapping; a mat is nothing but overlaps. Draw the crossings first and fill in around them. EACH FROND is a long triangular blade of bracken — a stiff central rib with paired leaflets stepping off it, each leaflet blunt and rounded at the tip, the whole blade tapering. The fronds are plainly UNEQUAL: some long and full, some short and half-grown, a few partly hidden under their neighbours. THE MAT IS FAIRLY CLOSED. Draw the smallest circle containing the patch and the fronds fill about THREE QUARTERS of it; within the inner four-fifths it is nearly unbroken. What gaps there are are small, irregular, and show DARK forest floor in shadow — never a clean wedge of background running in toward a middle. COLOUR: the deep green of shaded ground cover, matte and slightly dusty. A lit tone near #5E7F35, a body near #45632A, a shade near #24391A. ⚠️ IT MUST BE DARKER THAN THE TREES ABOVE IT, not brighter: this is what grows in the shade of a pine wood. Nothing here is acid, lime, chartreuse or fluorescent, and nothing is glossy — no specular highlights and no gradients, flat two-tone shading only. NO GROUND IS DRAWN and nothing stands up: the patch lies flat on a transparent background and the engine supplies the forest floor beneath it
assets.note: THE VENUE'S GROUND LAYER, and the one that will be placed most — bracken is what the open floor of a Minnesota pine wood is actually made of. See [[lake-alder-speckled]] for the underbrush family's ladder and shared reasoning. SIZE: 34u = 3.7 m across. A single bracken FROND is about a metre, but bracken grows in colonies and never as one frond, so what this sprite is is a small patch — which makes 3.7 m honest rather than exaggerated, and is the same argument [[ocean-grass-coastal]] uses for asking for two or three merged tussocks. ⚠️ IT IS ALMOST THE SAME VALUE AS THE GROUND IT LIES ON — L* 53.3 against the forest floor's 50.9, a difference of 2.4 — and it works anyway, at dE 38.8, because the separation is entirely HUE: a bright yellow-green frond on a warm brown floor. This is the second asset in the game to be built that way, after [[ocean-grass-coastal]], and the same warning applies: a delivery that comes back BROWNER or duller loses its only means of separation and disappears into the litter. Check hue before anything else. COLOUR-TWINNED WITH [[lake-birch-paper]] at dE 9.7 — both light yellow-greens. Separated on size (34u against 80u) and silhouette (flat triangular fronds against an open limbed crown), per art-pipeline 2. THE TRIANGLE IS THE ASSET. A fern drawn as a generic soft green rosette is a plant nobody can name; the divided triangular blade with a comb edge is recognisable at 34px and is the entire reason to spend a species on it. Reject a delivery whose fronds are undivided ovals. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, no allowSymmetry — a rosette of radiating fronds sits directly on the mandala attractor, which is why the subject asks for uneven lengths, uneven angles and a crossing frond rather than merely refusing a star. Plane `surface`, contact none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-15. Aspect 1.065, ONE connected clump, halo -0.33, mean #4D801C at dE 9.5 from spec. Ingest warned that content reached within 6% of the frame; fillTo 0.86 renormalises it and the clump is round in plan, so rotation is safe — that check is written for oblong content. THE TRIANGLE ARRIVED, which was the whole reason to spend a species here. The fronds are divided triangular blades with a comb edge and a clear midrib, at plainly uneven lengths and angles with one crossing a neighbour — recognisable as a FERN at 34px, where a generic soft rosette would have been a plant nobody could name. ⚠️ THE HUE-NOT-VALUE STRATEGY WORKED BETTER THAN PREDICTED. The slot expected this to sit within a couple of L* of the ground it lies on and to separate on hue alone; delivered it is 4.7 L* LIGHTER than the forest floor and clears it at dE 43.8, against a predicted 38.8. The floor's own delivery came back 7.5 L* darker than spec, which helped — the two errors happened to run in opposite directions. Green hue 96.1 at saturation 0.76, so it is the bright yellow-green asked for and not a dulled one. CIRCLE FILL 38.0% AGAINST THE ~60% ASKED — more open, and correct: a bracken clump is big flat blades with air between them. ⚠️ ANGULAR n=4 AT 51.3%, WELL OVER THE ACCEPTED COVE OAK'S 33%, AND IT IS THE FROND COUNT. Confirmed by the mirror test at LR 0.412 — statistically identical to the accepted [[ocean-pandanus]] at 0.405 and far below the accepted cove-oak-black at 0.696, so no symmetry is being faked. THIS IS THE FIFTH TIME THE POLAR METRIC HAS FLAGGED A SUBJECT BUILT FROM A SMALL NUMBER OF DISCRETE PARTS (pandanus n=3, ocean grass n=2, alder n=3, blueberry n=3, this n=4) and been wrong every time. The metric answers exactly one question — is this a ring of identical things around a hub — and any subject with a countable number of radiating members scores high on it honestly. Pair it with the mirror test as a matter of course. ⚠️ SUBJECT REWRITTEN 2026-08-16, AND THE REWRITE WAS OWED FROM AN EARLIER SESSION — it was described in conversation, reported as done, and never actually written. The delivery that arrived in the meantime therefore came from the OLD brief and cannot be held against the generator. THREE DELIVERIES, THREE SNOWFLAKES, AND THE BRIEF CAUSED ALL THREE. Shipped: alpha angular harmonic 42.2% at n=6. First reroll: 67.5% at n=6. Second: 44.9% at n=8. All three are radial rosettes, and all three are HONEST answers to a brief that asked for one clump of fern seen from directly above — because a single bracken fern from overhead genuinely is a rosette. The fix is not another prohibition, it is a DIFFERENT SUBJECT: a piece of a colony, fifteen fronds from plants whose centres are outside the picture. ⚠️ THE CROSSING CLAUSE IS THE POSITIVE EVIDENCE, borrowed from what worked on [[lagoon-coral-staghorn]]. Fronds in a rosette radiate and never overlap; a mat is nothing but overlaps, so a required four crossings is something a rosette CANNOT satisfy. Every other rule in this brief is a prohibition, and prohibitions can be dodged by a picture that simply avoids the issue. Ask for evidence instead. ALSO FIXED: the delivered fern measured L* 58.4 against the shipped 49.1 — nine points LIGHTER, in a venue already measured as too light against the game's own ladder (every temperate tree it ships sits between 23.8 and 40.2). Ground cover in a pine wood is the DARKEST layer, so the palette is now named and bounded. WHAT TO CHECK: alpha angular harmonic under 12% at every order 2-15; circle fill 0.70-0.80; interior ink above 90%; at least four visible frond-over-frond crossings; mean L* 42-48. ⚠️ ACCEPTED 2026-08-16 ON THE FIRST ROLL OF THE PATCH BRIEF. The snowflake is gone: worst alpha angular harmonic 12.2% at n=4, against 42.2% at n=6 shipped, 67.5% at n=6 and 44.9% at n=8 on the two rerolls before the rewrite. Ellipse fill 76.2% and interior ink 97.8%, both inside their windows. Frond-over-frond crossings are everywhere, which was the required evidence. Mean #42542C. ⚠️ TWO OF ITS FOUR CHECKS 'FAILED' AND BOTH FAILURES WERE MINE, NOT THE ART'S. (1) I wrote circle fill and circular interior ink into the checklist, then applied them to a subject with aspect 0.55 — the empty corners of the bounding circle counted against it, scoring 61.1% and 75.3%. Measured against the BOUNDING ELLIPSE, which is the only fair frame for a subject that is not round, they are 76.2% and 97.8%. USE THE ELLIPSE FOR ANY SUBJECT THAT IS NOT ROUND IN PLAN. (2) The L* window of 42-48 was set by shaving the previous delivery's 49.1, not by looking at the venue's ladder — the same mistake made on [[lake-birch-paper]]'s 55-63 window. The delivery came in at 33.6, which SATISFIES the stated intent ('darker than the trees above it': fir 23.8, white pine 35.9, red pine 38.2, aspen 52.1, birch 59.5) while missing the number. The intent was right and the number was wrong. Anchor windows on the ladder, never on the last delivery. ⚠️ ONE REAL COST, AND IT IS A COVERAGE COST NOT A PICTURE COST. Content came in 1.83x wider than tall, so ingest fires its NOT ORTHOGRAPHIC warning and the sprite renders 29x16px where the old one rendered 29x28px — about 58% of the inked footprint at the same world size. plant_lake.py models every plant as a FULL DISC of world x scale and never reads the sprite, so the venue's reported shrub coverage (23.6%) is now optimistic by roughly that factor. Same trap as [[lake-pine-white]]'s first delivery, in the opposite direction. Two ways out if the floor looks bare: raise `world` from 34 toward 45 and re-run --calibrate, or ask for a roll with squarer content. Neither is urgent — a bracken MAT is honestly not round in plan, and at play size the low wide patch reads better as ground cover than the old bright star did.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE LOW SHRUB, shot straight down from well above it. LOWBUSH BLUEBERRY — the knee-high woody mat that covers the thin dry ground between the pines and spreads out over bare glacial rock wherever there is a crack to root in. It is the SMALLEST and DENSEST of this venue's three underbrush plants. IT IS A LOW CLOSED MOUND: a compact cushion of small leaves packed tight, with no gaps you can see the ground through and no visible stem or branch anywhere. Where the mass parts you see hard-edged SHADOW INSIDE the plant, never a twig. Two or three of these cushions crowd together at plainly uneven sizes and merge where they touch, so the sprite reads as a patch of blueberry rather than one specimen — one clearly the largest, the others pushed off to one side. THE LEAF IS TINY, and that is what separates this from every other plant here. Small neat ovals, barely longer than they are wide, with a smooth edge and a fine point — drawn in dense overlapping groups so the surface reads as a fine pebbled texture rather than as countable leaves. Nothing about this plant is coarse. THE BERRIES ARE THE IDENTIFIER AND THEY ARE WORTH THE PIXELS. Scatter eight to fourteen small round BLUEBERRIES across the mound, a deep dusty blue with a pale bloom on them, sitting in loose bunches of two or three among the leaves. They are the only cool accent in this venue's planting and nothing else here is blue. A FEW LEAVES HAVE TURNED, which is true of lowbush blueberry from midsummer and is a cheap second accent: five or six single leaves in a warm crimson, scattered, never clustered and never on the outer rim where they would break the silhouette. THE GREEN IS A DEEP, CLEAN, SLIGHTLY BLUE-LEANING GREEN, darker than the fern and lighter than a fir. Build it from a lit tone near #338033, a body near #235C29, and a shade near #183D21 between the cushions. NOTHING HERE IS KHAKI, OLIVE, DUSTY OR GREYED-DOWN. AT THIS SIZE THE DETAIL BUDGET IS ABOUT TWENTY PIXELS ON SCREEN, so the leaf texture, the berries and the few red leaves are ALL that is asked for. Nothing else. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE, the rim is lumpy and bitten rather than a clean circle, and the plant fills about seven tenths of its own enclosing circle. NO WATER ANYWHERE, and no ground is DRAWN
assets.note: THE VENUE'S SMALLEST PLANT, for the thin ground between the pines and for the cracks in the [[lake-gneiss]] shelves — which is where lowbush blueberry actually grows, and is why the set has it rather than a second forest-floor plant. See [[lake-alder-speckled]] for the family's ladder. ⚠️ SIZE IS EXAGGERATED AND THE MANIFEST'S SCALE BLOCK REQUIRES THAT DECLARED: a lowbush blueberry plant is 0.3-0.6 m across, which is 3-6u and cannot carry a silhouette — the penguin argument. 22u is about 2.4 m, roughly a 4x exaggeration, and the subject compensates by asking for TWO OR THREE merged cushions so what is drawn is an honest patch at an honest size rather than one implausible bush. Same treatment as [[ocean-grass-coastal]] at 20u. THE BERRIES ARE THE ONLY COOL ACCENT IN THE VENUE'S PLANTING and are what earns this species its row at 22px, where the leaf texture will be nearly invisible. Blue against a warm brown floor is the strongest small-scale contrast available here — stronger than the alder's brown cones, which sit on a green plant. Colour that carries information wins under art-pipeline 3c even though nothing else in a pine wood is blue. COLOUR: L* 34.3, so the forest floor sits +16.6 above it, lake sand +37.4 and gneiss +26.5. Comfortable everywhere, and on the gneiss in particular it is the darkest thing on a light rock, which is what makes a boulder look planted rather than bare. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, no allowSymmetry. Plane `surface`, contact none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-15. Aspect 1.027, one connected patch, halo -0.10, mean #305B2D at dE 5.3 from spec — the closest colour match of the venue's underbrush. Circle fill 69.3% against the seven tenths asked, effectively exact. Same benign safeMargin warning as [[lake-fern-bracken]] and the same answer. THE BERRIES ARE THERE AND THEY ARE 4.2% OF THE SPRITE, in loose bunches among the leaves, with the turned red leaves at 2.2% — both inside what the subject asked for. They are the only cool accent in the venue's planting and the only blue anywhere in it, which is what earns this species its row at 22px where the leaf texture is nearly invisible. THE MERGED-CUSHION CONSTRUCTION ARRIVED, three cushions of uneven size grown together, which is what makes 22u an honest patch rather than one implausible 2.4 m bush — see the exaggeration note above. Reads +8.8 L* below the forest floor at dE 32.0, and dE 41.2 from [[lake-gneiss]], which matters because the rock cracks are half of what this plant is for: it is the darkest thing that will sit on a pale glacial slab, and that contrast is what makes a boulder look planted rather than bare. Angular n=3 at 42.1% is the cushion count, confirmed by the mirror test at LR 0.465 — see [[lake-fern-bracken]] for the full record on that metric.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no bark, no limb running away from you. A RED PINE — Norway pine, the state tree of Minnesota. ⚠️ THIS TREE IS NEVER SEEN ALONE. Several hundred of it stand shoulder to shoulder along a Minnesota lake shore, and its real job is to be one tuft in an unbroken forest canopy seen from the air. Judge it by that: the crowns must MERGE into a continuous rough green texture the way a boreal forest does in an aerial photograph. ⚠️ SO THE SILHOUETTE MUST NOT BE EXOTIC. From straight above, a north-woods tree is a ROUGHLY ROUND, RAGGED, CLOSED LUMP OF FOLIAGE. It is NOT a wheel, NOT a rosette, NOT a star, NOT a sunburst, NOT a snowflake, and above all NOT A PALM: no long separate fronds, blades, plumes or arms radiating out of a middle, and NO VISIBLE HUB OR CENTRE for anything to radiate from. If a viewer could count the arms, it is wrong. If the lighting makes bright lines run outward from the centre like the ribs of an umbrella, it is wrong. Break up any such radial pattern: the light in this crown falls in IRREGULAR PATCHES that have nothing to do with the middle. WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: A ROUNDED, COARSE, SLIGHTLY UNTIDY GREEN LUMP. Closed through the middle, bumpy round the edge, with a texture noticeably CHUNKIER than its neighbours — where the white pine is a soft cloud, this is a pile of thick bristly tufts pushed together. Draw the smallest circle that contains it; the foliage fills about SEVEN TENTHS of it, so it is a little airier than the white pine but still plainly a solid mass. ⚠️ IT IS NOT A STARBURST AND NOT A CATHERINE WHEEL. An earlier version of this brief asked for eight to fourteen separated needle-poms flung out around a centre; that is a PALM and it is refused. The tufts here TOUCH AND OVERLAP their neighbours. What openness there is takes the form of a few SHORT DARK NOTCHES bitten into the rim and one or two small ragged holes set OFF-CENTRE, never a wheel of gaps around a middle. THE TUFTS ARE THE TEXTURE. Fifteen or twenty rounded brush-heads of long paired needles, each with a bristled coarse edge that breaks into long fine points, packed across the crown at every angle with no pattern. Some sit high and catch the light; some sit low in shadow. The dark between them is a set of CROOKED CREASES that wander and never converge. THE COLOUR IS THE WARM GREEN OF THIS VENUE, and it is what separates this pine from the other two conifers. Build it from a lit tone near #6E8F42, a body near #4C6B33, and a deep shade near #26391D. That is an unmistakably YELLOW-GREEN, OLIVE-LEANING pine, warmer and lighter than the white pine's blue-green cloud and far warmer than the fir's near-black. NOTHING HERE IS TEAL, CYAN OR BLUE-GREEN. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE, round taken as a whole, lopsided in its bumps. NO WATER ANYWHERE, and no ground is DRAWN — the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the forest floor it stands on
assets.note: THE VENUE'S SIGNATURE TREE, and the fourth of Stillwater Lake's five. Minnesota's state tree, and what dominant forest stands, campgrounds, cabin lots and dry rocky ground are made of. ⚠️ 'SIGNATURE' IS ABOUT ABUNDANCE, NOT SIZE, and the distinction has to be stated because the two get confused when a planter is written. This is the tree to place MOST, and it is still not the biggest: eastern white pine genuinely out-spreads it in life, so [[lake-pine-white]] keeps 110u and this takes 88u. When the ocean's planter got its equivalent decision, abundance lived in GAIN and size in the species table; do the same here rather than inflating the crown to signal importance. SIZE IS HONEST: an open-grown red pine spreads about 9.6 m, and 9.6 x 9.2 units/m = 88u. Red pine is the narrower-crowned of the two big pines, which is why it sits below the white pine rather than above it. ⚠️ THE LADDER IS NOW FIVE DEEP AND COMPRESSED — 110 / 88 / 80 / 68 / 55, ratios 1.25 / 1.10 / 1.18 / 1.24 — well under the 1.33x the cove family holds. That is unavoidable with five trees and it is only safe because every ADJACENT pair is strongly separated on another axis: this against [[lake-pine-white]] at 1.25x is starburst tufts against stacked flat plates and dE 21.9 of colour; this against [[lake-birch-paper]] at 1.10x is a dark conifer against the venue's lightest broadleaf, dE 47. Anyone adding a SIXTH tree has to check its neighbours on both axes, because size alone can no longer carry it. SEPARATED FROM THE WHITE PINE ON THREE THINGS, and the subject spends its length on the first two: CONSTRUCTION (tufts flung out around spreading branches, against horizontal whorls read as stacked flat rafts), NEEDLE TEXTURE (long coarse brush against fine soft feathering), and COLOUR (warm yellow-green at hue 118, against blue-green at 150 — a real species difference, and the two subjects carry opposite tiebreaker instructions so a generator cannot split the difference). OPENNESS IS ASKED AT ~50% CIRCLE FILL, and that is pre-declared so a check written for compact crowns does not reject it — the same pre-emption [[lake-birch-paper]] and [[ocean-morning-glory]] needed. The brief's 'glimpses of ground beneath it' is the whole character of the tree. READS DARK ON ITS GROUND: crown L* 30.2 against the DELIVERED forest floor at 43.4, so the floor sits +13.2 above it at dE 38.4. Tighter than the +22 the spec floor would have given — see [[lake-forestfloor]], whose delivery came back 7.5 L* darker — but comfortable on dE, and this is a deliberately airy crown so the floor shows through it anyway. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, anchor trunk-base with no trunk drawn. NO allowSymmetry: a conifer from directly overhead is this library's strongest mandala attractor, and a crown built from radiating tufts is the exact shape that becomes a compass rose — cove-pine-pitch needed four rounds to beat this, which is why the subject states the construction and names the failure rather than merely refusing a star. PLANE `surface`, CONTACT none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ SUBJECT REWRITTEN 2026-08-15 BEFORE EVER BEING DRAWN. The original asked for 'eight to fourteen CHUNKY SEPARATED NEEDLE MASSES flung out around the centre' with 'the bare spreading branch lines and DARK GAPS' between them — which is a description of a palm, and is exactly the structure that made [[lake-pine-white]] read as a coconut grove. Caught by the aerial comparison before it cost a generation. See lake-pine-white's note for the root cause: species were over-separated on silhouette when they should have been separated on size and value. THIS PINE NOW CARRIES THE VENUE'S WARM GREEN. Three conifers need three answers that survive being seen in the hundreds, so they are separated on the two axes that aggregate: SIZE — fir 55u, red pine 88u, white pine 110u — and COLOUR — fir near-black blue-green, white pine mid blue-green, red pine warm olive. Silhouette is deliberately NOT a differentiator any more; all three are round ragged lumps.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE. A QUAKING ASPEN — the tree that fills in every clearing edge, old burn and roadside in the north woods, and this venue's general-purpose deciduous canopy. ⚠️ IT IS THE DENSE ONE, AND THAT IS ENTIRELY WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE BIRCH STANDING NEXT TO IT. A paper birch has an open airy crown you can see through, with its white limbs showing in the gaps. THIS CROWN IS CLOSED: the small leaves run together into CONTINUOUS ROUNDED MASSES of foliage, packed so the surface reads as one soft quilt with no gaps to see the ground through, no branch, no twig, and — this is the important part — NO PALE BARK VISIBLE ANYWHERE. An aspen's bark is pale greenish-white like a birch's, and from above you must not see one inch of it, because the canopy covers it. If limbs show through, the wrong tree has been drawn. THE LEAF IS SMALL AND ROUND. Nearly circular leaves with a bluntly toothed edge and a short point, drawn in dense overlapping clusters so the crown reads as a fine soft pebbled texture rather than as countable leaves. Nothing here is a big paddle or a long blade. The overall mass is built from six to ten SOFT ROUNDED LOBES that merge into each other, giving a full, rounded, gently bumpy outline — rounder and fuller than any other tree in this venue. THE SHIMMER IS THE SPECIES' NAME AND IT IS A TEXTURE, NOT A SEASON. Aspen leaves are hung on flattened stalks and turn in the lightest air, so a real crown is always flecked with leaves catching the light at a different angle from their neighbours. Show this as SMALL SCATTERED PATCHES OF PALER YELLOW-GREEN through the canopy — a dozen or so, each a handful of leaves, spread unevenly and never pooling into one bright side. ⚠️ THIS IS NOT AUTUMN. No gold, no orange, no amber, no bare twig, and no patch so pale it reads as a turning leaf: the paler flecks are the SAME green seen brighter, not a different colour. A tree that looks like it is changing has failed this clause. THE GREEN IS A MEDIUM-LIGHT GREEN, COOLER AND GREYER THAN THE BIRCH, and that difference is doing real separation work — these two are the same size class and both are round broadleaves, so colour and density are what tell them apart. Build the tree from a lit tone near #7FBF63 on the crowns that catch the sun, a body near #599949 through the mass, and a deep shade near #2E5A28 in the hollows between lobes. NOTHING HERE IS THE BRIGHT YELLOW-GREEN OF A BIRCH, nothing is the blue-green of a pine, and nothing is olive, khaki, dusty or drab — cooler means slightly toward BLUE and slightly less saturated, never toward grey mud. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE, and the crown fills about eight tenths of its own enclosing circle — this is a full tree. The rim is softly lobed and irregular, never a clean disc. NO WATER ANYWHERE, and no ground is DRAWN — the tree is alone on a transparent background
assets.note: THE VENUE'S GENERAL-PURPOSE DECIDUOUS CANOPY — secondary woodland, disturbed ground, regrowth, and the edges of large clearings. Fifth and last of Stillwater Lake's trees. SIZE IS HONEST: a quaking aspen spreads about 7.4 m, and 7.4 x 9.2 = 68u. Narrower than the paper birch above it, as it is in life. See [[lake-pine-red]] for the five-deep ladder and why it is now compressed. ⚠️ THE BIRCH IS THIS SLOT'S ONLY REAL RISK AND THE SUBJECT ATTACKS IT DIRECTLY. They are adjacent in the ladder at 1.18x, both round broadleaves, both pale-barked in life, and both in the same wood — the most confusable pair in the venue by a distance. Three things separate them and only the first survives colour removal, which is what art-pipeline 2 actually requires: DENSITY. The birch is asked for ~50% circle fill with white limbs showing through the gaps; this is asked for ~80% with a closed canopy and an explicit instruction that no pale bark may be visible anywhere. That inversion is deliberate and it is the whole design — it also means a delivery here that shows limbs has drawn a birch, and should go back however good it looks. Colour carries the rest at dE 18.6, cooler and greyer per the brief. THE SHIMMER CLAUSE IS THE SECOND RISK. 'Pale patches through the canopy' is one word away from autumn, and this library has been bitten by exactly that shape of ambiguity before — [[ocean-almond-tropical]] needed a hard bound on its crimson leaves for the same reason and came in at 3.5% against a 12% reject line. So the clause states the PHYSICS (flattened stalks, leaves turning in the air), gives the correct read (the same green seen brighter), and names the failure (gold, orange, amber, bare twig). CHECK THE WARM FRACTION ON DELIVERY: anything above a few percent of warm pixels means it has turned, and the tree is supposed to be in full summer leaf. READS AGAINST ITS GROUND THE OTHER WAY UP: crown L* 57.5 against the delivered forest floor at 43.4, so it is 14.1 L* LIGHTER than the ground, at dE 40.6. Stillwater is the venue whose canopy runs both directions — two dark conifers, two light broadleaves, and a fir darker still — which is what [[lake-forestfloor]]'s medium value exists to carry. planRound true, fillTo 0.86, no allowSymmetry. PLANE `surface`, CONTACT none when the art lands. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-15. Aspect 1.001, one connected crown, mean #60904B at dE 8.0 from spec, halo -0.21. Ingest warned that content reached within 6% of the frame edge; fillTo 0.86 renormalised it to 87.9% fill with a 5.9% margin, and rotation is safe anyway because the crown is round in plan — the safeMargin check is written for oblong content. ⚠️ THE BIRCH SEPARATION IS DELIVERED AND IT IS THE DESIGN WORKING. This slot's only real risk was confusion with [[lake-birch-paper]]: adjacent in the ladder at 1.18x, both round, both pale-barked in life. The separator was density, inverted on purpose. Measured on what shipped: this is 83.4% circle fill with a closed canopy and no bark visible anywhere, against the birch's 44.4% with its limbs showing through. That is a 2x difference on the one axis that survives colour removal, which is what art-pipeline 2 asks for; colour adds dE 16.1 on top, cooler and greyer as briefed (hue 105.0 at saturation 0.49, against the birch's 74.4 at 0.60). THE SHIMMER CLAUSE HELD: warm pixels measure 0.0%. The pale flecks came back as the same green seen brighter, which is what the subject demanded, and nothing turned. That clause was written defensively after [[ocean-almond-tropical]] needed a hard bound on its crimson leaves; on this asset it cost nothing and the risk did not materialise. Reads LIGHT on its ground — 11.6 L* above the forest floor at dE 37.1 — which is the other half of what [[lake-forestfloor]]'s medium value exists to carry. Angular n=8 at 24.3%; mirror 0.858, high for the same honest reason [[lake-fir-balsam]] scores high, a compact round mass. ⚠️ SECOND ASPEN, 2026-08-15, TAKEN AS A PARTIAL FIX AND RECORDED AS ONE. The brief was to bring the lightness down; it moved L* 55.2 -> 52.1, sat 0.49 -> 0.48, hue 101.8 -> 99.2. The structure is better — the clumps now carry real tonal separation instead of reading as one even field of bright poms — and fill/interior/radial all hold (81.6% / 99.3% / 1.00). Master arrived 2816x1536 and was square-cropped to 1558px on the content bbox before ingest. ⚠️ IT DOES NOT CLOSE THE GAP, and the honest yardstick is THIS GAME, not the photographs. The reference aerials put a Minnesota canopy at L* 25.9-38.6, but the house style is deliberately brighter than a photograph, so that comparison alone would have been a bad argument. The internal ladder makes the same case and makes it properly: every TEMPERATE tree the game ships sits between 23.8 and 40.2 (fir 23.8, cove-pine-pitch 29.0, white pine 35.9, red pine 38.2, cove-oak-black 40.2), and the 42-53 band belongs to the LAGOON PALMS. At 52.1 this aspen is still in palm territory — brighter than every lagoon palm but the coconut, and twelve points above the lightest temperate tree in the game. It wants about L* 45, which would seat it just above cove-oak-black as the lake's light broadleaf without being the brightest thing in the game. ⚠️ AND THE SAME ARGUMENT INDICTS A WINDOW I SET MYSELF. [[lake-birch-paper]] was accepted against an L* 55-63 window and delivered 59.5 — the lightest tree in the entire game, above every palm. Its job is to be the pale tree that lifts a dark conifer wood, and against white pine at 35.9 it would do that just as clearly at 50. The 55-63 window was set by looking at the birch alone rather than at the ladder it had to join, which is the same mistake in miniature as briefing the three trees to be distinguishable from each other.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. A WOODEN LAKE DOCK, the plain crib-and-plank kind every Minnesota cabin has, seen from above and ALONE — no water under it, no shore, nothing but the structure. IT RUNS THE LENGTH OF THE FRAME, pointing to the TOP, and its two long edges are exactly PARALLEL — the far end is the same width as the near end, nothing tapers or converges, and no end face or side of a post is visible. It is about eight times as long as it is wide. THE DECKING IS THE SUBJECT: a run of separate PLANKS laid ACROSS the dock, side by side down its whole length, each one a long flat board with a hard edge and a narrow dark gap to its neighbour. Vary them — a few boards a shade greyer, one or two a shade warmer, one slightly cupped — so the deck reads as sawn timber and not as a striped ribbon. Down each long edge runs a slightly darker STRINGER, the frame board the planks are nailed to. At the far end, the tops of two or three POSTS show as small dark squares just outside the deck line. A few small dark nail heads. Nothing else is on it: no cleat, no ladder, no rope, no boat, no chair, no bucket. THE WOOD IS WEATHERED GREY-BROWN, not fresh lumber and not painted. Build it from a lit plank near #B3A48E, a body near #9A8B76 and a shade near #6E6153 in the gaps between boards. NOTHING HERE IS ORANGE PINE, RED CEDAR, VARNISH, WHITE PAINT OR GREEN TREATED TIMBER — this is sun-and-ice weathered softwood, silvered by ten winters. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no reflection, no wet stain, no ripple. The dock is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the lake around it
assets.note: STILLWATER LAKE'S WATERFRONT, and the first of nine built and natural props for the venue. ⚠️ FOUR OF THIS BATCH ARE LONG AND DIRECTIONAL — this, [[lake-cabin]], [[lake-log-fallen]] and [[lake-canoe]] — and that changes two things about how they are declared and placed. planRound is FALSE on all four, so prompt.py gives them the ORTHO_LONG acceptance test (parallel sides, no convergence) instead of the roundness one, which would otherwise instruct a generator to square up a subject that is honestly 8:1. And they must be placed with the editor's `prop-spin` checkbox OFF and a `heading` set per placement, the cove-town rule: a dock has a direction that means something — it runs OUT from the shore — and a scatter of randomly spun docks reads as wreckage. SIZE: 12 m long, and 12 x 9.2 units/m = 110u. Matches the swamp's own dock at 108u, which is the same object for a different water. PLANE `surface`, following swamp-dock: a deck is above the water and the fleet goes AROUND it, so it is not `float` (that plane is for things ON the water that land covers — a lily pad, a raft) and not `canopy` (nothing sails under a dock). ⚠️ CONTACT hard WHEN THE ART LANDS, and the contactR must be measured off the BAKE rather than guessed. This is the case the cargo-ship note warns about: an 8:1 object cannot be covered by one circle. Sized to the length it is an invisible wall standing 50u off both sides in open water; sized to the beam it leaves most of the dock sailable through. Take the beam — under-covering is the safer error, because a pass-through is a missed collision while an oversized circle is the unfairness the shoal note argues against. swamp-dock's answer is contactR 9 with an srcBox, and that is the model to copy. COLOUR SITS BETWEEN ITS TWO GROUNDS: dE 42.7 from the lake water it mostly stands over, but only 10.6 from [[lake-sand]] where it crosses a beach. That is the weak case and it is accepted, because a dock is a strongly LINEAR object — parallel edges and a plank rhythm read at a glance where a colour difference would not. If it ever reads flat against a beach, darken the gaps between boards rather than the boards. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED 2026-08-15 AND INGESTED, BUT IT IS NOT THE OBJECT THE SLOT ASKS FOR, and the defect is the one number this asset is built around. The subject says 'about eight times as long as it is wide' and the size line derives world 110 from 12 m of LENGTH. Delivered content measures 1442x2636, an aspect of 1.83:1, so at world 110 it bakes to 95px long by 52px in the beam — a 12 m x 6.5 m platform rather than a 12 m x 1.5 m walkway. CONFIRMED ON THE CONTACT SHEET, where it reads as a raft: at 110px there is no length to it, nothing about it runs OUT from anywhere, and the whole reason this asset is placed with prop-spin OFF and a per-placement heading — that a dock has a direction that means something — has nothing left to act on. THE CONSEQUENCES ARE NOT COSMETIC. contactR was to be taken at the beam per the cargo-ship rule, i.e. about 9 following swamp-dock; at this aspect the beam is 26, so the collider triples and the 'under-cover rather than over-cover' reasoning stops applying because there is no longer a long axis to under-cover. A second, smaller problem rides along: at 110px the ~34 cross planks land at 2.8px each and moire into the striped ribbon the subject explicitly asks the art not to become. EVERYTHING ELSE IS RIGHT and is why this was ingested rather than dropped — true plan view, edges parallel with no convergence, planks laid across, stringers down both long edges, no cleat or ladder or rope, and the weathering is on the money: lit-half median measures dE 4.2 from the declared body #9A8B76, with none of the orange pine or varnish the subject forbids. So this is a PROPORTION regeneration, not a redraw — keep the palette and the construction, ask for 8:1. Until then the shipped file is a swim platform wearing the dock's key. RESOLVED 2026-08-15 — ACCEPTED AS A PLATFORM DOCK, world 110 -> 42, and the new number is MEASURED OFF THE ART rather than assumed. Two independent readings agree. The deck carries 30 boards at an 87px pitch, and at a standard 14-16cm deck board that is 4.2-4.9 m of length. The crib posts read 90px square in a 1442px beam, i.e. 6.2% of it, which at the same scale is a 15cm timber — a 6x6 crib post, exactly right. Both put the object at about 4.5 m x 2.5 m, so world = 4.5 x 9.2 = 42 and the drawn dock is 36 x 20px. Note this is well under the ~60 first estimated when the decision was framed: that figure came from holding the declared 12 m LENGTH and letting the beam inflate to 6.5 m, which the plank and post measurements both refute — a 6.5 m beam would need 40cm crib posts. THE SIZE LINE ABOVE IS NOW WRONG and is kept for the record: this is no longer 12 m and no longer matches swamp-dock's 108u. It is the small crib platform a cabin actually has, and the venue is short a long walkway if one is ever wanted — that would be a new slot, not a regeneration of this one. CONTACTR FALLS OUT AT ABOUT 10, which is the pleasing part: the beam is 20px drawn, so half of it is 10, and the cargo-ship rule (take the beam, under-cover rather than over-cover) lands within a unit of swamp-dock's contactR 9 by a completely different route. THE MOIRE PROBLEM WENT AWAY WITH THE SIZE. At world 110 the 30 cross planks fell at 2.8px each and shimmered into the striped ribbon the subject warns against; at world 42 the deck is 36px long and the planks read as a texture rather than as lines, which is the honest outcome — the moire was a symptom of drawing a 4.5 m object at 12 m. Placement guidance stands unchanged: prop-spin OFF, heading per placement, running out from the shore.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. A SMALL LAKE CABIN seen from straight above, ALONE — no ground, no trees, no path, nothing but the building. ⚠️ YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF, AND THE ROOF IS ALMOST THE WHOLE PICTURE. From directly overhead a building is its roof: two rectangular slopes meeting along a RIDGE that runs the length of the cabin and points to the TOP of the frame. The two slopes are equal, the ridge is a clean line down the middle, and the eaves overhang each long side by a little — so a thin band of LOG WALL shows below each eave, and nothing more of the walls than that. No wall face, no window seen side-on, no porch post standing up. The building is about a third longer than it is wide, and its long edges are PARALLEL — nothing converges. THE ROOF IS DARK GREEN STANDING-SEAM METAL, the roof half the cabins in the north woods have: flat panels with fine straight SEAM LINES running down the slope from ridge to eave, evenly spaced, a shade darker than the panel. One slope catches the light and is slightly lighter than the other. Build it from a lit slope near #4E7048, a shade slope near #3D5A3A and seams near #2A3F2A. A STONE CHIMNEY at one end, seen from above as a small rectangle of grey fieldstone breaking the ridge line. A short covered PORCH at one gable end, reading as a smaller rectangle of the same roof projecting from it. Under the eaves, the log wall shows as a narrow warm brown band near #7E5C3C with the round ends of the logs just visible at the corners. NOTHING ELSE IS DRAWN: no path, no steps, no deck furniture, no washing line, no smoke, no vehicle, no fence. NO GROUND AND NO CAST SHADOW — the cabin is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the forest floor it stands on
assets.note: THE VENUE'S ONE BUILDING, for cabin lots and camp waterfronts. Size 9.6 m long, and 9.6 x 9.2 = 88u — between the cove's Cape cottage (80u) and its dormered cottage (100u), which is the right company. ⚠️ THE ROOF IS THE ASSET AND THE WALLS ARE NEARLY INVISIBLE, which is what saves this slot from a colour collision it would otherwise have. A log cabin's WALLS measure dE 5.5 from [[lake-forestfloor]] — a warm brown building on warm brown ground, effectively camouflaged. But from directly overhead you see almost none of them: what you see is the roof, and a dark green metal roof sits dE 26.3 from the same floor. So the subject is written as a roof with a band of wall under the eaves, which is both what the camera actually sees and what makes the building read. Anyone who ever re-specs this with a shingle or shake roof has to re-check that number — a brown roof would disappear. DIRECTIONAL, and it matters more here than for anything else in this batch: a building has a ridge, and a scatter of cabins with ridges pointing every which way reads as wreckage. See [[lake-dock]] for the shared placement rule. planRound false — it is a third longer than it is wide and gets the parallel-sides acceptance test. PLANE `surface`, CONTACT none: it stands on land the fleet cannot reach, so the collider would never be tested, and the cove's whole town ships on exactly that argument. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ DELIVERED 2026-08-15 AND REJECTED — NOT INGESTED, status stays `slot`. The delivery is a SIDE ELEVATION, which is precisely the failure the subject's loudest clause exists to prevent and the one art-pipeline records as unfixable by asking harder. Four independent tells, any one of which settles it. THE RIDGE RUNS ACROSS THE FRAME rather than pointing to the top, so even read generously the object is rotated 90 degrees from the declared orientation. A FULL WALL FACE IS DRAWN: the lower 55% of the building is a flat green board-and-batten face, where the subject allows 'nothing more of the walls than' a thin band of log under the eaves. THE FOUNDATION PIERS SHOW THEIR SIDES AND THEIR FEET along the bottom edge — from directly overhead a pier is a dot, and seeing the length of one means the camera is looking at the long side of the building. And the CHIMNEY IS A BOX WITH A FRONT FACE rather than the small grey rectangle breaking the ridge. Content measures 2499x1300, aspect 1.92, against the 1.33 the plan calls for ('about a third longer than it is wide') — the excess is the wall the camera should not be able to see. Roughly 60 degrees off vertical by eye. THE MATERIAL LANGUAGE IS ALL CORRECT — dark green standing-seam metal with fine seam lines, stone chimney, log ends, a porch projecting at one gable end — so this is a CAMERA regeneration and the subject text needs no rewrite. Worth noting for whoever re-runs it that this is the batch's hardest subject for exactly the reason the pipeline states: buildings are overwhelmingly photographed from the side, and a prompt that says 'straight down' politely loses to that prior. The tree batch needed the same fight. ⚠️ SECOND DELIVERY 2026-08-15 — ACCEPTED, AND THE FIRST READ OF IT WAS WRONG. It looks at a glance like the same elevation the first delivery was rejected for: a lighter green plane on top, a darker green plane below, and brown log work along the bottom edge. It is not, and TWO MEASUREMENTS SETTLE IT where the eye could not. FIRST, THE RIDGE SITS AT 49%/51% of the body — two equal slopes meeting down the middle, exactly what the subject asks. SECOND AND DECISIVE, THE SEAM PITCH MATCHES ACROSS THE RIDGE: 25.5 px above against 25.7 px below, within 1%. That is the foreshortening test, and it is the one an elevation cannot pass — on a side view the roof plane is raked away from the camera and the wall is square to it, so their seam pitches differ by the cosine of the tilt. Equal pitch means both halves are the same plane at the same obliquity, i.e. TWO ROOF SLOPES. The dark lower half is the shaded slope the subject asks for ('one slope catches the light'), at 101.5 against 62.2 mean luma. Long edges are parallel: width 1846 px at the top against 1868 at the bottom, a net 1.4% over the body, so ORTHO_LONG passes with no convergence. ROTATED 90 DEGREES CCW ON INGEST and that is the only pixel change made. The delivery has the ridge running ACROSS the frame; art-pipeline 3 requires anything with a front to face the top, and for a gable that is the ridge. CCW rather than CW because it also lands the lit slope on the left, matching this venue's measured convention — 11 of 13 shipped lake props carry their highlight up-left. A free, lossless fix for what would otherwise be a regeneration. TWO DEVIATIONS ACCEPTED. The roof plan is 2.13:1 where the subject says 'about a third longer than it is wide' (1.33) — a longer cabin than specified but an honest one. And the log-wall band shows below ONE eave rather than both, which is the fingerprint of a small residual tilt; the equal seam pitch caps how small. ANCHOR LEFT AT THE SEEDED BBOX CENTRE deliberately: the porch pulls the main roof mass 2.2% off it, but the porch is part of the building's footprint, so correcting to the roof centre would move the anchor 1.9 px at world 88 in arguably the wrong direction.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. ONE FALLEN TREE TRUNK lying on a forest floor, seen from above and ALONE — no ground drawn, no leaves, nothing but the log. IT LIES ALONG THE FRAME, pointing to the TOP, and it is about eight times as long as it is wide. Its two long edges run very nearly PARALLEL, tapering only slightly from the root end to the top end — the far end is nearly as wide as the near end, and no cut face or end grain is visible except as a small ellipse at each end. IT IS AN OLD DEAD TREE, NOT FRESH TIMBER. Along its length the BARK has come away in irregular patches: where it remains it is a rough dark grey-brown with coarse vertical furrows; where it has fallen off, the bare WOOD shows through as a smoother, paler, silvery grey-tan. Four or five such bare patches of plainly uneven size, with soft ragged edges, scattered unevenly down the trunk rather than in a row. The top surface catches the light and is a shade lighter along the crown of the log; the two long sides roll away into shadow, so a narrow darker band runs down each edge. That roll is the only modelling — it is what makes a cylinder read from above. A FEW BROKEN BRANCH STUBS stick out at uneven angles, three or four, short and blunt. At the root end, a small ragged mass of broken roots. Patches of dull grey-green LICHEN and a little MOSS on the upper surface, soft-edged, more of it toward the shaded end. The wood runs from a lit crown near #7E6B52 through a body near #5E4A33 to a deep shade near #3A2E20 down the sides, with the bare patches a paler silvery grey near #8E8272. NOTHING HERE IS ORANGE, FRESHLY CUT, PAINTED OR CHARRED. No ground, no shadow, no undergrowth, no mushrooms, no water. The log is alone on a transparent background
assets.note: FOREST-FLOOR FURNITURE — a blowdown lying in the woods, and the cheapest way to break up an otherwise even stand of trees. 8 m long, and 8 x 9.2 = 74u. ⚠️ NOT [[swamp-driftlog]], WHICH IS A DIFFERENT OBJECT FOR A DIFFERENT PLACE. That one is a deadhead: waterlogged, half-submerged, on the `float` plane with contact hard, and it exists to be hit. This lies on dry ground in a forest, on `surface` with contact NONE — it is scenery on land the fleet cannot reach, so a collider here would never be tested. The two are dE-close in colour and could not be less alike in what they do; anyone reaching for one should check which question they are answering. DIRECTIONAL and planRound FALSE, at roughly 8:1 — see [[lake-dock]] for the shared rule on both. A log wants its heading set per placement anyway, because a scatter of logs all pointing the same way looks planted and all pointing randomly looks like a game asset; the truthful answer is a few lying downslope and the rest anyhow. THE ROLL IS THE ONE PIECE OF MODELLING THAT MATTERS. A cylinder seen from directly above is a rectangle, and the only thing that says it is round is a lighter crown with the two long sides falling into shadow. Without it this reads as a plank, which is exactly what [[lake-dock]] is — and those two must not be confusable, being 74u and 110u of similar colour. The dock is flat, hard-edged and made of separate boards; this is one continuous rolled mass with ragged bark. Check that first on delivery. Colour sits dE 13.5 from the forest floor it lies on — the tightest of this batch, and acceptable because a log is a strong linear form on a mottled ground. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ DELIVERED 2026-08-15 AND REJECTED — NOT INGESTED, status stays `slot`. What arrived is A STANDING DEAD SNAG SEEN FROM THE SIDE, not a blowdown seen from above, and it fails on the camera, the proportion and the object all three. CAMERA: the cut face at the top is drawn as a full open ellipse with visible depth, and the branch stubs show their end grain the same way — from directly above, the end of a HORIZONTAL log and the stub of a sideways branch are both edge-on and collapse to slivers, which is the same foreshortening rule [[lake-bulrush]] just failed and the cypress moss failed before it. OBJECT: the trunk FLARES 1.36x toward the bottom into a root base spreading onto ground. That is a tree still rooted where it grew; a fallen log has two ends and no base, and the subject asks for a small ellipse at EACH end. PROPORTION: content measures 527x1436, an aspect of 2.72:1, against the 'about eight times as long as it is wide' the slot asks and the 8 m / 74u size line derives from. The taper clause fails with it — 'two long edges very nearly PARALLEL, tapering only slightly' against a 36% flare. THE SURFACE TREATMENT IS EXACTLY RIGHT and should be kept in the re-prompt: bark come away in four or five irregular pale patches with ragged edges, coarse vertical furrows where it remains, lichen and a little moss low down. So this is a CAMERA AND FRAMING regeneration on good material. Alpha was clean (real, 89% transparent, no white stroke), so nothing about the cut needs saying to the generator. SECOND DELIVERY 2026-08-15 — ACCEPTED AND INGESTED. This is the object the slot asked for, and the two measurements that mattered both pass. TRUNK ASPECT IS 6.6:1 against the 'about eight times as long as it is wide' asked — and note the trap: the raw content bbox is 2455x757, which reads as 3.2:1 and looks like a hard fail, but 757 is the span INCLUDING the branch stubs projecting either side. The trunk's own median thickness is 374 px, and length over that is 6.6. Measure the trunk, not the bounding box. Taper across the body is 1.26x, which is the 'very nearly parallel' the subject wants. CAMERA CONFIRMED BY SHADING, ALBEDO-CONTROLLED. A raw cross-axis luminance profile said 'monotonic gradient, side view' and was WRONG, because the big pale bare-wood patches sit in the upper half and swamped the shading with albedo. Restricting to BARK pixels gives a hump: 71.9 at the upper edge, peaking 80.4 at 0.3 across the width, falling to 43.0 at the lower edge. Bright crown offset toward the light with BOTH flanks rolling into shadow is the plan-view signature; a side view has no second shadow. Control for albedo before reading shading on anything with patchy colour. THE END FACE MEASURES ABOUT 8 DEGREES OFF VERTICAL, not the 47 the first automated pass reported — that mask keyed on pale low-saturation pixels and ate the grey-green lichen sitting just inboard of the cap. Off the crop the end cap is roughly 52 px along the axis against a 370 px trunk, so sin(tilt) = 0.14. Well inside the 'small ellipse at each end' the subject permits. ROTATED 90 DEGREES CCW ON INGEST, the only pixel change, for the same two reasons as [[lake-cabin]]: art-pipeline 3 wants the long axis pointing to the top, and CCW puts the lit flank on the left to match the venue's up-left convention. Splintered break ends up at the bottom, clean end at the top. Contact stays NONE per the note above, so the 6.6:1 collider problem [[lake-dock]] had never arises here.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. ONE CANOE, seen from straight above and ALONE on a transparent background — no water, no wake, no reflection, no shore, no paddler. IT POINTS TO THE TOP OF THE FRAME and it is about five and a half times as long as it is wide. THE HULL IS A SYMMETRIC LEAF SHAPE: both ends come to the same fine point, the beam is at the middle, and the two sides curve identically. A canoe has no bow and no stern to tell apart from above — if one end is blunter or wider than the other, the wrong boat has been drawn. YOU ARE LOOKING INTO AN OPEN BOAT, which is the whole read at this angle. Down the middle runs the dark open COCKPIT — the inside of the hull, a long leaf-shaped well in deep shadow, taking up most of the deck. Around it runs a narrow pale GUNWALE, a clean rim following the whole outline. Across the well lie THREE THWARTS — plain straight cross bars, evenly spaced — and at each end a small triangular DECK PLATE closing the point. One wooden seat visible near each end. Inside the hull, fine RIB lines run across the floor at even intervals, catching a little light. A single PADDLE lies along one side inside the boat, a plain shaft with a flat blade. Nothing else: no motor, no bag, no rope, no person, no fishing rod. THE HULL IS A WARM CEDAR-RED CANVAS, the classic north-woods canoe: a lit tone near #CB8A4E on the outside of the hull where the light falls, a body near #B5713A, and the cockpit shadow near #4A2E19. The gunwale, thwarts, seats and ribs are pale varnished ash near #D9BE8C. NOTHING HERE IS WHITE, GREY, ALUMINIUM, NEON, OR THE FLAT PLASTIC OF A MODERN KAYAK. The silhouette must be a clean, symmetric, sharp-ended leaf. No sail, no mast, no rig of any kind
assets.note: THE VENUE'S SMALL CRAFT — the card's hazards line already promises 'islands, skiffs and shoals', and this is the skiff. 5 m long, and 5 x 9.2 = 46u. ⚠️ ROLE IS `traffic`, WHICH BINDS IT UNDER art-pipeline 2: it MUST NOT be confusable with a competitor at race scale. Three things carry that and they are all in the subject. NO RIG — the single most reliable separator, because every racing boat in this game is a triangle of sail and this is a bare open hull. AN OPEN COCKPIT taking most of the deck, where a dinghy shows a foredeck and a mast step. And SIZE, at 46u against the fleet's 32u. The swamp's pirogue sets the precedent at 62u and ships; this is the same object one venue north. SYMMETRIC ENDS ARE THE SPECIES MARK and the subject states it twice, because every generator has far more kayaks and rowboats in it than canoes and both of those have a distinguishable bow. A canoe from above is a leaf. PLANE `float` WHEN THE ART LANDS, and this is the one plane call in the batch worth stating: `float` is the plane that answers 'water object'. It draws after every mark the water makes — swell, wakes, cat's-paws — so nothing ripples across a hull floating on top of it, and BEFORE the land, so a beach simply covers the part of a drawn-up canoe that lies on it. That last property is free and is exactly what a canoe hauled halfway out wants. CONTACT soft, contactR about 6 measured off the bake: a canoe is light and a racing hull would shove it aside rather than stop dead, which is the pirogue's answer too. COLOUR IS INFORMATION AND IT IS LOUD ON PURPOSE: cedar-red sits dE 74.8 from the lake water, the strongest separation of anything in this batch. A canoe is a small object on open water and it has to be seen. planRound FALSE at 5.5:1 — see [[lake-dock]]. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND INGESTED 2026-08-15, AND IT PASSES THE ONE TEST THIS SLOT EXISTS TO WORRY ABOUT. SYMMETRY, the species mark the note flags twice because generators hold far more kayaks and rowboats than canoes, is measured at 99.9% fore/aft mirror agreement and 99.8% port/starboard, with maximum beam at 47% of the length. Neither end is blunter than the other; it is a leaf. The content list is complete and contains nothing extra: open cockpit taking most of the deck, pale gunwale following the whole outline, three thwarts, a triangular deck plate closing each point, a seat near each end, rib lines across the floor, and one paddle along one side. No rig, no motor, no person. CONFUSABILITY CLEARED WITH COLOUR REMOVED, which is what art-pipeline 2 actually demands and what the contact sheet alone does not show. Against a competitor at race scale: in greyscale the canoe is a narrow dark spindle and the racing hull is a broad shape carrying a bright white sail wedge down its length; squinted (greyscale plus a 2.2px blur) the two stay unmistakable. NO RIG does the work exactly as predicted, and the beam difference helps rather than hurts — the 46u canoe is visibly NARROWER than the 32u competitor even while being longer. Colour is loud as intended: hull to lagoon water dE 92.3, to arctic 61.3. Palette lands near the declared tones (lit hull dE 8.5 from #CB8A4E, trim dE 9.5 from #D9BE8C); the cockpit came back DARKER than #4A2E19 by dE 17.1, which reads correctly as a deep open well and was kept. ⚠️ THE HULL IS BEAMIER THAN SPEC: content measures 2455x626, an aspect of 3.92:1 against the 5.5:1 asked, so at world 46 it draws 40px long by 10px in the beam where 7px was intended. In real terms that is a 5 m canoe carrying a 1.28 m beam instead of 0.9 m — a fat tripping canoe rather than a wrong boat, and invisible at 40px. Accepted as delivered and world left at 46, because unlike [[lake-dock]]'s 1.83-against-8 this is a 1.4x error that does not change what the object IS. If it ever wants correcting, an anisotropic squeeze on the beam axis is the cheap fix and costs no regeneration. ROTATED 90 DEGREES CCW ON INGEST, the only pixel change: art-pipeline 3 wants the bow at the top, and CCW also lands the lit flank on the left, matching the up-left convention 11 of 13 shipped lake props already carry. Symmetric ends mean the rotation has no wrong choice.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. ONE LARGE GLACIAL BOULDER — a granite erratic, the kind the ice left standing on its own all over the north woods — seen from directly above and ALONE, with no ground drawn around it. IT IS ROUNDED, NOT BROKEN. This stone spent a hundred thousand years under moving ice and every edge on it has been worn soft: from above it is a broad irregular LOBED BLOB, wider than it is neat, with a couple of shallow bays in its outline and no straight edge and no sharp corner anywhere. It is NOT angular rubble and it is NOT a shattered block. THE DOME IS THE MODELLING. It is a rock sitting on the ground, so its crown is nearest the camera and lightest, and its colour steps DOWN in two or three flat bands as the stone rolls away toward the edge — clean hard-edged steps, no soft gradient. Push the lightest crown plainly OFF-CENTRE so the boulder is lopsided rather than a target. THE MINERAL IS THE SAME GNEISS THE SHORE IS MADE OF: cool medium grey, with one or two broad soft BANDS of warm dusty pink feldspar and a rusty iron-stained brown sweeping across it, and a narrow charcoal band. Restrained — a grey rock with colour IN it, not a colourful rock. Two or three thin CRACKS wander across the crown, curving and irregular, never a grid. In the hollows, a little pale crusty LICHEN as a faint soft paling of the stone's own colour, and a small patch of dull moss on the shaded side. Build it from a lit crown near #A29DA3, a body near #8A858B and a shade near #605C63 at the rim. NEVER the warm grey-tan of a New England headland, never black basalt, never orange sandstone. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. No water, no waterline, no wet stain, no cast shadow, no ground
assets.note: ROCKY POINTS, TINY ISLANDS AND THE OCCASIONAL ERRATIC STANDING IN THE FOREST. 4.8 m across, and 4.8 x 9.2 = 44u. Its sibling [[lake-boulder-small]] is 18u, a 2.4x step, so the two never read as one asset at two scales. ⚠️ IT IS THE SAME STONE AS [[lake-gneiss]] AND MEASURES dE 4.3 FROM IT, WHICH IS CORRECT AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED'. A boulder on a granite shelf is the same rock as the shelf; if it read as a different material the venue's geology would be wrong. What separates a boulder from the ground is SHAPE and MODELLING — a lobed blob with a lit off-centre crown stepping down to a dark rim, against a flat tiling surface — not colour. Where it needs to be seen it is: dE 23.5 against [[lake-sand]] and 30.6 against [[lake-forestfloor]], the two grounds it will actually be placed on. CONTACT hard WHEN THE ART LANDS, with contactR at the drawn radius — and this is the one prop in the game where a circular collider is exactly right rather than a compromise. The cargo-ship note has to argue itself out of colliders because a 4.3:1 hull cannot be covered by a circle; a boulder IS a circle. It is also visible, which is the other half of the shoal note's fairness test: you cannot decide to avoid something you cannot see, and this you can. planRound true, plane `surface`. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED 2026-08-15 PRE-CUT, AND THE CUT CARRIES A WHITE STICKER STROKE — the one thing about this batch that needed work. The remover left real alpha with a soft ~14px feather, but a pure-white outline is painted around the silhouette underneath it: 36k px of RGB 255,255,255 sitting at alpha 1-60. Two reasons that cannot ship. It is faintly visible as a pale rim over forestfloor, and worse, ingest downsamples 2048->1024 with a plain channel-by-channel RGBA resize, so white under near-zero alpha is averaged into every edge pixel on the way down — the bayou-cypress halo lesson with the sign flipped (black there, white here). A FLAT ALPHA CHOKE CANNOT SEPARATE THEM, which is what the first attempt assumed: along one ray the stone's own RGB survives down to alpha 101 and the white starts at 73, but around the rest of the perimeter white reaches alpha 160 (p99 of the 130-160 band is 244). Any single threshold either keeps white or eats stone. UNMIX DOES SEPARATE THEM. At a partial pixel the stored colour C is the stone F and the stroke W=255 sharing the stored coverage a, so the stone's own coverage is the projection s = a*dot(C-W, F-W)/|F-W|^2 clamped to [0,a], with F estimated by growing confident stone colour (alpha>0.85, not near-white) outward under the fringe. RGB is then replaced by the recovered F, so no white survives at any alpha — MEASURED: zero near-white px above alpha 12, against 36k before, and the partial-alpha band's luma p99 falls to 106/113. Silhouette is unmoved (bbox 1714 -> 1710 of 2048, 0.2%). Colour-bled 22px outward afterwards for the same reason bayou-cypress is: the resize has no idea the alpha is zero. INGEST CLEAN — no ORTHOGRAPHIC warning (bbox is 1.000/1.001, the roundest pair in the library), no margin warning, only the expected 2048->1024 downsample note. THE PREP IS NOT COMMITTED TOOLING and the delivered files are not in the repo; they are on the Desktop as large-boulder.png and Gemini_Generated_Image_yd8f1myd8f1myd8f.png. The inbox copy is the PREPPED file, so re-running ingest on it is idempotent and does not need the unmix again. ⚠️ THE REST OF THE LAKE BATCH HAS THE SAME STROKE AND SHIPPED WITH IT — lake-pine-red's master still carries 9.5k px of white at alpha 1-10 and 6.4k at 10-60. Left alone deliberately: at world 22-110 the band is sub-pixel, which is the arctic-orca-calf finding (a 1.7x fringe is invisible below ~130px). Worth a re-prep only if a lake tree ever grows past that. GEOLOGY CONFIRMED BY MEASUREMENT rather than by the slot's estimate, and it lands where the slot said it would: dE 5.7 against lake-gneiss (predicted 4.3 — same stone, correct, do not 'fix'), 20.7 against lake-sand and 27.6 against lake-forestfloor (predicted 23.5 and 30.6). The venue's rock reads as one material and the boulder still separates from both grounds it gets planted on. DRAWN RADIUS IS 19px, NOT 22 — fillTo 0.86 means world 44 draws a 38px stone — so contactR is 19 for whoever registers this in PROP_KINDS. ⚠️ THE WARM BANDS ARE LOUDER AT RACE SCALE THAN IN THE MASTER. 14.5% of opaque px sit above chroma 40 (median 8, p99 90), and at 44px the rust and feldspar sweeps read as bright rings rather than as the 'grey rock with colour IN it' the subject asks for — closer to banded than restrained on sand and forestfloor both. Accepted as delivered because it is legible, correctly lit and unmistakably a rounded stone, but this is the one open judgement on the pair and a desaturation pass on the bands is the fix if it grates in the venue.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. A SWIM RAFT — a square wooden float anchored off a cabin beach — seen from straight above and ALONE, with no water drawn around it. IT IS A SQUARE, as tall as it is wide, with slightly rounded corners and a plain flat deck. The DECKING is separate PLANKS laid side by side across it, each a long flat board with a hard edge and a narrow dark gap to its neighbour, running edge to edge in ONE direction only. Around the whole deck runs a slightly darker rim board. ON IT, AND ONLY THESE: a small ALUMINIUM LADDER at one edge, seen from above as two short parallel rails with three rungs between them, projecting a little past the deck. Two dark ANCHOR CLEATS at opposite corners with a short length of rope on each. Nothing else — no towel, no chair, no diving board, no person, no logo. THE WOOD IS SUN-BLEACHED AND PALE, lighter than a shore dock because it stands in open water all summer: a lit plank near #C8BAA2, a body near #B0A088, and a shade near #7E7462 in the plank gaps. Under the deck, just visible past the rim on two sides, the dark tops of the FLOAT BARRELS as two or three flat dark bands. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no ripple, no reflection, no wake, no wet stain, no waterline. The raft is alone on a transparent background
assets.note: THE CABIN WATERFRONT'S OTHER HALF, sitting fifty metres off the beach. 3.6 m square, and 3.6 x 9.2 = 33u.
