assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A HIGH FOOTBRIDGE, shot straight down — the picture a survey tile makes of a crossing. THE BRIDGE RUNS UP AND DOWN THE FRAME, its deck along the tall axis, both ends stopping short of the edges. ⚠️ IT IS DEAD STRAIGHT, AND THIS IS THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT. The deck runs in a single straight line from one abutment to the other. Its two long edges are PARALLEL for the entire span and its centreline does not wander: lay a ruler along either edge and it touches from end to end. NO bend, no kink, no S-curve, no dog-leg, no gentle curve, no sag, no twist. A crooked deck is the failure this clause exists to prevent and it is the most likely wrong answer. ⚠️ AND IT CROSSES HIGH — high enough that a sailing boat with its mast standing passes underneath it. In a picture taken from straight above, height cannot be drawn, so it is shown by what is ABSENT: there is NO pier, no piling, no trestle, no post, no strut and no support of any kind anywhere between the two ends, and NOTHING touches the river. The deck flies clear from one bank to the other in one unbroken run, and the only things carrying it are the two abutments at the very ends, which sit back on dry ground. If anything stands in the water, the bridge has been drawn low and it is wrong. WHAT A BRIDGE LOOKS LIKE FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE, and this is the test that proves the camera: you see the WALKING SURFACE and nothing else of its height. No underside, no side of any beam, no face of any abutment — an abutment reads as a flat pad lying at the end of the deck, never as a block standing up beside it. Nothing tapers or converges: the far end of the deck is exactly as wide as the near end. ⚠️ IT IS A NARROW RIBBON. The deck WITH its two handrails is about one TENTH of the total span across — wide enough for one walker to cross, and no wider. If it comes back a third or a fifth as wide as it is long it is a road bridge, a pier or a boardwalk, not a hiking bridge. Long and thin is the whole silhouette. THE DECK IS PLANKED CROSSWISE, so from above it reads as a long ladder of short transverse boards, each board a separate flat shape with a thin dark line between it and the next, running the entire length. That regular banded deck is the identifying feature and it is SUPPOSED to be even and repeating — it is joinery, not scattered scenery — so the boards run at a steady pitch the whole way across. A few planks sit slightly paler or darker than their neighbours so the timber is not uniform, but the SPACING stays regular. A HANDRAIL RUNS DOWN EACH SIDE — from above, two thin continuous lines just inside the deck edges, dead parallel to them and to each other, with slim posts at regular intervals reading as small dark ticks along them. At each end the deck meets a low ABUTMENT of stacked grey stone, a squarish pad a little wider than the deck, and the two abutments match each other. THE TIMBER IS WEATHERED GREY, not fresh lumber and not painted: a lit plank near #A9A498, a body near #8B8578, a shaded plank near #6A6459, with the stone abutments cooler and greyer near #8E939A. NOTHING ELSE: no water, no river, no bank, no path, no people, no pier, no piling, no cutwater, no shadow, no reflection, no cables, no suspension towers, no arch below the deck. No ground is drawn: the bridge is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies what it crosses.

The subject closed with 'IT IS SLIGHTLY CROOKED, because it is a backcountry structure: the deck line has one gentle bend in it rather than being dead straight' — and prompt.py had already appended ORTHO_LONG two paragraphs earlier, which says 'its two long edges must run PARALLEL for its whole length ... nothing tapers, narrows or converges'. Those two argue, and the generator resolved it the way prompt.py's own portrait note says it always does: by dropping one half. Charm is not worth a contradiction. SECOND, `allowSymmetry` WAS MISSING AND THE DECK IS JOINERY. ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE appends 'evenly spaced, symmetrical arrangement, tiled pattern' to every asset without that flag, and this subject's identifying feature is a ladder of evenly spaced transverse planks — so the prompt asked for regular spacing and refused it in the same breath. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH SHOT STRAIGHT DOWN FROM WELL ABOVE, the geometry of an orthophoto. ONE SMALL BACKPACKING TENT pitched on a gravel bar, seen from directly above and ALONE. It is a two-person dome tent: from straight overhead a rounded-cornered rectangle about ONE AND A HALF TIMES as long as it is wide, with its long axis running UP the frame. That ratio is the number to hold — it is a stubby oblong, not a long thin shape and not a circle — and its two long sides run roughly parallel down the frame without tapering, because you are directly above it. THE TWO POLES ARE THE IDENTIFYING FEATURE AND THEY CROSS. From above you see them as two slim arcs running corner to corner over the canopy, meeting at a low peak just off the middle — that X is what makes this read as a tent and not as a boulder or a bag. The fabric between them is divided into four gently curved panels, each a single flat tone, brighter on the two panels either side of the peak and stepping down toward the corners as the dome falls away. A SMALL VESTIBULE — a lower triangular flap of the same fabric — projects from one long side, which makes the outline asymmetric, and that asymmetry matters because the engine spins this and a symmetric dome would read as a stamped repeat. Four short guy lines run out from the corners as fine taut lines ending in tiny pegs. THE COLOUR IS THE ONE MANUFACTURED THING IN THIS VENUE AND IT IS ALLOWED TO BE BRIGHT: a warm saturated expedition ORANGE-RED — a lit panel near #E2653A, a body near #C24B26, a shaded panel near #8E3418 — with the vestibule a shade darker and the poles reading as thin pale grey lines over the fabric. Nothing else in Sockeye Run is a manufactured colour, which is exactly why this one is worth its pixels. NOTHING ELSE: no person, no campfire, no pack, no boat, no gravel, no shadow, no second tent. No ground is drawn and no cast shadow: the object is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies what it sits on.
assets.note: THE HUMAN PRESENCE, AND IT IS TWENTY-TWO PIXELS OF STORY. Sockeye Run is a salmon river; people camp on its bars to fish it, and one small tent on a gravel bar tells you that in a way no amount of vegetation can. It is the only manufactured object in the venue. ⚠️ ITS COLOUR IS THE POINT AND IT BREAKS THE PALETTE ON PURPOSE. Everything else in this venue is granite grey, water teal, or one of six greens; the one loud exception is [[river-fireweed]]'s magenta. An expedition orange-red (#C24B26) is dE 60+ from every ground here and reads instantly at 22px, which is exactly art-pipeline 3c's 'colour that carries information always wins ... even when that colour appears nowhere else in the venue'. A tent in a muted natural colour would be a grey lump on grey gravel and would not be worth the slot. THE CROSSED POLES ARE THE IDENTIFIER. At this size a dome tent and a boulder are both rounded blobs; the X of the two pole arcs over the canopy is the only thing that separates them, so the subject leads with it. The vestibule flap makes the outline asymmetric, which matters because prop-spin is ON and a symmetric dome would read as a stamped repeat once several are placed. PLACE IT IN ONES, on dry bars and terraces near the water, never in the forest and never more than two or three on the whole course. contact none — it is above the waterline and the fleet cannot reach it. THE EIGHT ARE ONE COMMISSION AND THEY FILL THREE GAPS THE VENUE HAD. Sockeye Run shipped with seven plants, four grounds and nothing else: no rock you can hit, no wood, and no sign that a human being has ever been there. The boulders give the card's own 'Rocky banks' hazards line something to point at, the log and the jam are the two most conspicuous objects in the owner's West Susitna reference after the trees themselves, and the bridge and tent are the whole of the venue's human presence. ⚠️ THE BOULDERS ARE NOT THE `outcrop` TERRAIN AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH KEEPING. `outcrop` is a SHAPE — 44 of them are authored in river.venue.js, equivalent diameters 54 to 1022 u, median 135 — and it means a scoured bedrock ledge standing out of the rapids. These are PROPS, and they mean individual stones. The largest boulder here is 52u, deliberately just under the smallest existing outcrop polygon, so the two families never compete: ledges are terrain, stones are props, and the size ladder says which is which without anyone having to explain it. ⚠️ AND THEY ARE NOT [[lake-boulder-large]] EITHER. Stillwater's is a glacial ERRATIC — 'rounded, not broken ... every edge worn soft ... a broad irregular LOBED BLOB'. This is the opposite geology: canyon granite that the ice planed flat and the frost then cracked apart, so it is an ANGULAR block with a flat scoured top and clean facets. The subjects name the rounded pebble as the failure precisely because the two venues would otherwise converge on the same stone. SCALE: at 9.2 px/m the ladder is 5.7 m, 3.7 m and 2.2 m for the three dry boulders, which is honest for river granite and needs none of the exaggeration the plants take. The large one is very nearly one boat length (56u), which is the most useful size reference the venue has. PLANES: `surface` for the dry boulders, the log and the tent — they sit on ground, under the fleet. `seabed` for the sunken boulder, so the water above it does the colouring, following the lagoon corals. `float` for the logjam, which rides ON the water and must draw after the water's own marks so no wake ripples across it. `canopy` for the footbridge, because that is the plane for a thing the fleet passes UNDER. Prop-spin ON for the boulders, the log and the tent; OFF for the bridge, which has an axis the placement must control. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ planRound FALSE AND THE PROPORTION IS STATED IN THE SUBJECT, because 1.5:1 is the awkward middle of prompt.py's two acceptance tests. planRound true would demand 'as tall as it is wide' of a thing that honestly is not, and ingest would fail it at the 1.12 bar; planRound false hands it ORTHO_LONG's 'much longer than it is wide ... parallel for its whole length', which overstates a stubby dome. So the subject names the ratio outright, which turns a vague clause into a number and keeps the prompt from arguing with itself. ⚠️ world RAISED 22 -> 44 ON DELIVERY, 2026-08-22, AND THE ORIGINAL FIGURE WAS THE MISTAKE — NOT THE ART. 22u is the honest size of a two-person backpacking tent (2.4 m x 9.2), and at 18 px on screen it is an anonymous orange smudge: the crossed poles that are its entire identity are gone, and it could be a buoy, a flower or a paint blob. Rendered up a ladder on cobble and meadow — 22, 30, 36, 44, 56u — the pole X first appears at 36u/30px and the thing is unambiguously a TENT at 44u/37px. 56u was tried and rejected: that is alder size and a tent as big as a thicket is silly. 44u is 4.8 m, about a 2x exaggeration, which is modest in a venue where willow runs 1.75-3x and the moss mat 2-3x, and it is exactly the case manifest.json's own scale note licenses: 'a penguin's true overhead footprint is ~0.5m = 4.6px, which cannot carry a silhouette. Exaggerate deliberately and record it here; do not drift.' Recorded here. ⚠️ AND IT MOVES THE TENT UP THE VENUE'S LADDER, which is the cost worth stating: at 44u it now sits between [[river-willow]] at 30 and [[river-alder-red]] at 56, so a camp reads as roughly bush-sized rather than as a speck. That is the right trade for the one object in Sockeye Run that carries a story, but it does mean a tent must never be placed in a thicket where it would be read as a shrub.

scale.anchor: The player's boat. Hull is ~56 world units (see the repositionBoats comment in script.js) and the camera is 1:1, so 56px = one boat.
scale.boatLength: Treat the boat as a ~20ft (6.1m) sportboat. Nothing in the game names a class, so this is a free choice — and it is the one that makes the accepted art self-consistent. At J/105 scale (10.5m) everything already accepted would be ~2x oversize.
scale.note: Exaggeration is permitted and often required: a penguin's true overhead footprint is ~0.5m = 4.6px, which cannot carry a silhouette. Measured on arctic water, a 7-bird huddle needs ~70px before individual birds resolve and species colour appears. Exaggerate deliberately and record it here; do not drift.

variance.source: hash(index, channel) — deterministic, never Math.random, so the render path cannot perturb the RNG stream the eval harness depends on

notes: surfaceDepth is deliberately NOT zero — a swimming orca is never fully out of the water, and bottoming the depth curve at 0 draws it flat on the surface like a decal.
The depth curve DWELLS: rise, swim up top, sink, stay down. A sine spends equal time everywhere and reads as bobbing.

Deep animals draw as a flat dark silhouette (#0a1a2c via source-atop), not as the faded real sprite. Losing the markings is what reads as UNDER water; a faded sprite reads as merely far away. Drone footage shows the opposite — markings persist at depth — but legibility at 40px beat accuracy here.

The blow is emitted in WORLD space at the animal's position when it blew, and stays put while the animal swims on. Evaluated analytically from past time, so there is no particle list and nothing to reset between races.
Blow density peaks at exhalation and only falls. Holding peak opacity while the sprite scales up reads as fading IN, which is a bug that took three passes to see.
Rejected after trying: bow wake, submerging foam, fluke prints as rings, and fluke prints as bubble scatters. All read as graphics rather than water.
